findings.paper_title: 6a. CTB Report 27-28 M&C Draft - PASC Copy

findings.detail: The report describes Government changes to council tax collection, including reminders and final notices before a household loses the right to pay in instalments. It also notes that default 12-month billing starts for newly liable taxpayers in April 2027 and for all others from April 2028.
findings.matters: Changes to enforcement timing and billing affect how quickly arrears build and recover, which bears on the collection rate a council budgets for.

findings.detail: The current discretionary relief policy dates from 2017. Its cost is shared through the business rates retention system, and any changes will be reported back to Council before taking effect in 2028/29.

findings.detail: The report recommends no change to the scheme for 2027/28. It states that the forgone revenue is met through reductions in spending in other areas of the council.
findings.matters: The scheme's cost is a large revenue item, and the report shows it is being absorbed by cuts elsewhere, which a finance director would compare with their own scheme cost and funding approach.

findings.detail: The Business Rates Baseline is being reviewed as part of the 2027/28 Local Government Finance Settlement, so the council's top-up or tariff may change. The paper says the settlement is expected in the week commencing 14 December 2026.
findings.matters: Top-up changes move the council's retained business rates funding directly, and the outcome will show how the Business Rates Retention reset affects a London borough.

findings.quote: The full impact of this will not be known until the Settlement is released in mid-December 2026.

findings.matters: Business rates are a major income line, and the report shows the council is using a provisional figure while the reset and Autumn Budget changes are still unresolved, which a lender or peer would want to track.

findings.matters: The mix of savings types shows how much of the programme depends on demand reduction rather than on budget cuts, which affects how confident a finance director can be in the delivery.

findings.matters: The gap-to-target arithmetic shows how a shortfall in one year's savings and an in-year overspend add up to a required total that another council could compare against its own.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Equipment and NHS Health Checks efficiencies total £62,500, with £25,000 from the Public Health Grant and the rest from unused inflation provision.

The NHS Health Checks saving of £25,000 comes from the Public Health Grant and is described as the release of set-aside inflation funding that has not been needed.
findings.matters: Releasing inflation provision that was not needed is a budgeting point other councils setting inflation allowances on contracts will recognise, and the jointly funded equipment contract is a model used across other councils with ICBs.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: A new 13-year leisure contract is expected to contribute approximately £350,000 towards savings targets from 2029/30.
findings.detail: The paper says the income increase is contractually agreed rather than aspirational, following financial modelling and affordability checks during procurement. The text places the increase from 2029/30 onwards, but the savings table places the £350,000 in the 2028/29 column, which the paper does not reconcile. The management fee commitments are stated as unaffected by actual income achieved.
findings.matters: Income from a long leisure concession is a contractual stream other councils with similar outsourced leisure contracts will compare, and a 13-year term is a long-dated commitment a lender would want to see reflected in its contract exposure.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Adult Learning Lewisham plans a £234,808 investment from ring-fenced reserves, with income gains totalling £143,000 to the general fund.
findings.detail: The investment would fund a new pottery studio, a classroom conversion on the second floor of the Brockley Rise centre, and alterations to enable income generation. The income components are £48,000 from the pottery studio (year two, after capital works), £27,000 from a 50p per hour fee increase, £20,000 from raising room hire targets from £40,000 to £60,000, and £48,000 from moving language classes into income-generating provision. The paper notes the service would need to rebuild ring-fenced reserves to mitigate skills-funding risk.
findings.matters: Drawing ring-fenced reserves to fund an invest-to-save case, with the paper itself flagging the need to replenish them, is a reserve-use decision other councils with grant-funded adult learning services will recognise.
findings.figures: £234,808 investment; £143,000 total savings to the general fund; £48,000 pottery studio income (year two); £27,000 fee increase; £20,000 room hire; £48,000 language classes; room hire target £40,000 to £60,000
findings.quote: The investment would total £234,808 from the services ringfenced reserves.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Review of 1:1 care in residential and nursing placements is proposed to save £1,000,000 in 2027/28 and £500,000 in 2028/29, with the paper rating deliverability higher risk in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper describes a continuing programme of intensive reviews for people receiving 1:1 care in care homes, often linked to dementia-related behaviours that challenge, with joint funding and Continuing Healthcare processes used where health needs apply. The paper says the approach is already in place and delivering the intended outcomes, and that the 2028/29 saving is higher risk because it depends on year-on-year delivery. The overall risk is rated amber.
findings.matters: The 1:1 care line is one of the larger savings in the appendix and depends on the health and social care funding split, which a finance director would want to see tested against the NHS contribution.
findings.quote: This approach is already in place and delivering the intended outcomes.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Enablement proposal aims to manage demand within in-house capacity rather than outsource it, with a net saving of £100,000 a year over 2027/28 to 2029/30.
findings.detail: The paper says approximately £1m a year is spent buying enablement care from external domiciliary providers, and that the in-house service is more effective at supporting independence. Efficiencies already achieved or agreed are £181k in 2025/26 and £357k in 2026/27 against spot purchased and longer-term care. The proposal may involve a dedicated enablement contract, which would need hourly-rate pricing and KPIs.
findings.matters: Shifting spend from spot-bought domiciliary care to an in-house or contracted enablement model is a change other councils managing homecare costs will compare against.

findings.quote: Approximately £1m is spent annually on purchasing care in this way.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Shared Lives extension to people with dementia and self-neglect is estimated at £539,000 a year net of staffing cost, phased over two years.
findings.detail: The proposal is an invest-to-save scheme, with an additional Shared Lives officer and a Business Support Officer costing c£85,000 moved from existing budgets. The aim is at least four more carers and at least ten more placements. The net saving is £227,000 in 2027/28 and £312,000 in 2028/29, reflecting the time to recruit and approve carers.

findings.quote: A saving of £539,000 per annum is estimated net of the additional staffing cost

findings.headline: Better Care Fund uplift of 4.4% against a 3% pay award produces a £156,111 saving that can be made recurrent from 2027/28.
findings.detail: The 2026/27 Adult Social Care uplift within the Better Care Fund was 4.4%, of which 3% was needed for the Council's pay award. findings.quote: This resulted in a saving of £156,111 which can be made a recurrent saving from 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Analysis in March 2026 identified approximately £1 million a year of funded but unused learning disability placements, with a £250,000 saving in 2027/28 from reducing them.
findings.detail: The paper says voids cost about £1m a year, mainly in block contracts where the total cost of all places is included. The new framework will pay 50% of void costs rather than 100%, with a 12-week limit on void payments.

findings.quote: Analysis in March 2026 identified approximately £1 million in annual expenditure on funded but unused placements

findings.paper_title: 4c. Appendix 3 - Healthier Communities Select Committee Proformas
findings.headline: Complex care placements estimated at approximately £12m per annum carry an estimated £2m overspend across partners, and the Complex Care Recovery Programme is framed around cost avoidance rather than cashable savings.

findings.matters: A finance director, here or at a peer council, would want to know how a jointly funded placement overspend is being recovered and whether the savings in the template are cashable or avoidance figures.

findings.quote: with an estimated £2m overspend across partners

findings.detail: The paper says 100 on-street chargers from the ORCS scheme are being installed and the LEVI project will deliver a further 1,150 from late 2026 to 2030. The risk section notes that LEVI is 'just finishing procurement', and that the cross-pavement charger pilot may reduce demand.
findings.matters: A finance director would see an income target tied to a contractor-led rollout that has not yet started at scale.
findings.figures: £50,000 in 2027/28 and £50,000 in 2028/29; 1,250 chargepoints; 100 ORCS chargers by end 2026; 1,150 LEVI chargers
findings.quote: LEVI is just finishing procurement with rollout likely to commence later in the year.

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham's Public Realm Efficiencies proposal makes a £10,000 saving in 2027/28 from replacing a hired excavator with a council-owned one and sets a £40,000 saving for 2028/29.
findings.detail: The excavator would come from the 2027/28 Fleet Replacement Programme at an estimated £30,000 capital cost. The proposal also includes a Bereavement Services fee increase, and the risk section notes a £50,000 Fleet Replacement Plan contribution as a fallback funding route.
findings.matters: A finance director would see a hire-to-buy swap funded from the fleet programme, with a named capital source and a fallback.
findings.figures: £16,000 annual hire expenditure; £6,000 retained; £10,000 revenue saving; £30,000 capital purchase; £40,000 in 2028/29
findings.quote: replace the hired excavator used for earth burials at Grove Park Cemetery with a council-owned excavator already included in the 2027/28 Fleet Replacement Programme.

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham plans to remove its non-statutory Local Meetings from the planning process, with a £35,000 saving in 2027/28 and the paper stating that 20 of the last 28 applications considered by committee would now be automatically delegated.
findings.detail: The paper says Lewisham is 'nationally gold rated' for planning performance but that this is underpinned by extensions of time, which Local Meetings require. The change needs an update to the Statement of Community Involvement, which is a Key Decision with a public consultation requirement.
findings.matters: A finance director would see a saving tied to a performance metric that the Government is expected to tighten, and a change that requires legal consultation.
findings.figures: £35,000 net saving in 2027/28; 20 of 28 applications over the last 10 committees; 'gold rated' planning performance
findings.quote: From the last 10 planning committee meetings (A and B), which considered 28 applications, 20 of those would now be automatically delegated.

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham's Strategic Planning consultancy budget is proposed to fall by £50,000 in 2027/28, with the paper noting a '£93,600' general fund allocation and four reviews identified by the Local Plan inspectors.
findings.detail: The inspectors instructed immediate reviews of four documents, with approximate costs of £30,000, £30,000, £20,000 and £30,000. Officers consider the reviews not legally required before a formal Local Plan review, which is expected to start in 2028/29 at the earliest, and the paper records reputational risk if the inspector's instructions are not followed.
findings.matters: A finance director would see a saving that defers evidence work the Local Plan inspectors asked for, with a stated reputational and cost-award risk at appeal.
findings.figures: £93,600 general fund allocation; £50,000 saving in 2027/28; retained budget £43,600; approximate study costs £30,000, £30,000, £20,000 and £30,000
findings.quote: The Local Plan was adopted in July 2025. During the examination of the Local Plan the inspectors instructed the Council to undertake immediate reviews of several key documents

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham plans a £162,000 saving in 2027/28 and a further £67,000 in 2028/29 by charging planning application fees to recover Strategic Planning costs.
findings.detail: Local fee-setting is expected under national legislation not yet published, and the saving assumes continued development management income. The paper says planning income in 25/26 'has been relatively healthy' but that income for 27/28 and 28/29 is 'very challenging to predict'.
findings.matters: A finance director would want to see a fee-driven saving that depends on application volumes and on a national power that has not yet been brought into force.
findings.quote: Planning income in 25/26 has been relatively healthy and we are relatively confident that this will continue into 26/27.

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham's Millwall lease restructure is expected to add £50k a year of rental income from 2027/28, and a Copperas Street Heads of Terms with L&G a further £50k fixed income during pre-development.
findings.detail: The Millwall uplift is described as secure on a 999-year stadium lease, with additional ground rent not assumed. The L&G Heads of Terms were approved by the Council in January 2026 and carry a risk that the income falls away if planning permission for the modelled scheme is not secured after five years.
findings.matters: A finance director would see new commercial property income that is partly contingent on planning, and lenders would note a stated end date on the certainty of the L&G income stream.
findings.figures: £50k pa Millwall uplift from 27/28; £50K fixed income in pre-development; c£100k assumed annual rental on the commercial unit; 2027/28 net saving £100,000; 5 years of certainty
findings.quote: The terms agreed provide for 5 years of certainty. Beyond that, if no permission is secured, that income stream will fall away.

findings.paper_title: 4f. Appendix 7 - Sustainable Development Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Lewisham proposes a £375,000 saving in 2027/28 from cutting highways drainage, carriageway and footway maintenance, which the paper rates High impact.
findings.detail: The proposal ends the borough-wide proactive gully and drain cleansing programme and reduces planned carriageway and footway repairs. The paper states the Key Decision route applies and that the change 'materially reduces planned preventative maintenance'.
findings.matters: A finance director elsewhere would want to see how a council funds a statutory highway duty when it cuts planned maintenance, and what deferred revenue and claims costs it has put on the table.
findings.figures: £375,000 net saving in 2027/28 (£75,000 gully cleansing, £200,000 highways and footways maintenance, £100,000 recharge); the Risk section refers to a '£275,000 saving'
findings.quote: The proposal materially reduces planned preventative maintenance across highway drainage, carriageways and footways, while retaining a risk based and reactive response.

findings.paper_title: 4h.Appendix 9 - All proposals by theme
findings.headline: HSG-01 Reduction in temporary accommodation costs is shown at £2,000,000 in each of 2027/28 and 2028/29.
findings.detail: The proposal is a reduction in temporary accommodation costs and is the same in both years. The table does not explain how the reduction would be achieved.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation costs are a widely reported pressure on councils, so a saving of this size held flat across two years would interest peers in the same position.

findings.headline: CR-09 Employers Pension Contribution Reduction is shown as £4,000,000 in 2027/28 and nil in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The saving appears only in the first year, so it does not carry into 2028/29. The table gives no reason for the reduction in employer contributions.
findings.matters: A one-year saving from pension contributions would need replacing in the following year, which matters to any council relying on it in its medium-term plan.
findings.quote: CR-09 Employers Pension Contribution Reduction 4,000,000.00£

findings.paper_title: 4h.Appendix 9 - All proposals by theme
findings.headline: CYP-03 Placement Sufficiency, Family Intervention and Demand Management Programme is the largest single proposal, at £5,360,000 in 2027/28 rising to £5,930,000 in 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper lists this demand-management programme for children and young people as the largest line in both years. It is titled as a placement sufficiency and family intervention programme. The table does not show the mechanism.
findings.matters: Children's placement costs are a common pressure at councils, so a finance officer elsewhere would want to see how much of a budget gap rests on one demand programme.
findings.quote: CYP-03 Placement Sufficiency, Family Intervention and Demand Management Programme 5,360,000.00£

findings.paper_title: 4h.Appendix 9 - All proposals by theme

findings.detail: The appendix lists proposals across Adult Social Care & Health, Children and Young People, Corporate Resources, Place and Chief Executive. The totals row gives the sum for each year. The table is headed as proposals, so the figures are not yet confirmed savings.
findings.matters: A finance director here or at another council can compare the size of the gap being closed and how much of it falls away after the first year.

findings.paper_title: 4e. Appendix 6 - Safer Stronger Communities Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Community Services Efficiencies proposes a 2027/28 saving of £64,593, including removal of a £12,000 Food Safety contingency and a £10,000 pool car saving.
findings.detail: The package combines three items: removing a £12,000 annual Food Safety contingency for major incidents, a possible £10,000 saving from removing one of four pool cars, and a renegotiated Forced Entry SLA. The paper says any additional emergency costs would have to be met within the Environmental Health budget or become an overspend.
findings.matters: Removing an emergency contingency moves the risk of an unplanned statutory cost into the service's own budget, which a finance director would want to track against any later overspend.
findings.figures: £64,593 net saving in 2027/28; £12,000 annual Food Safety contingency; £10,000 per pool car per year
findings.quote: have to funded from within the EH budget or be an overspend.

findings.paper_title: 4e. Appendix 6 - Safer Stronger Communities Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Home Library Service proposes an £80,000 annual saving in 2027/28 by moving from a dedicated delivery team to a volunteer-led model, with the change fully implemented by 1 April 2027.
findings.detail: The saving comes from reduced staffing costs and the release of three leased fleet vehicles. The paper says five volunteers would be recruited to deliver to about 150 housebound residents, with the transition beginning in December 2026 and a vacant post deleted after December 2026.
findings.matters: It is a service-delivery saving that relies on recruiting unpaid volunteers, and the paper names that recruitment as the point of failure, so a finance director could see the saving depend on a non-cash assumption.
findings.figures: £80,000 annual saving in 2027/28; 3 leased fleet vans released; about 150 residents; five volunteers
findings.quote: the new volunteer-led model fully implemented by 1 April 2027.

findings.paper_title: 4e. Appendix 6 - Safer Stronger Communities Select Committee proformas
findings.headline: Main Grants Programme proposes a £126,000 General Fund saving in 2028/29, the final year of the three-year grant cycle awarded on 1 April 2026.
findings.detail: The paper says the programme was awarded for 2026-29 with a value of £1,575,746 per annum, and that the saving would come from a review of the Neighbourhood and Borough-wide strands. It describes this as the first in-year reduction to grants of its kind and records the risk level as High.
findings.matters: A council proposing to cut a multi-year grant programme part-way through its cycle, when the grant agreements permit it, shows how finance directors are treating voluntary-sector funding as a flexible savings line.
findings.figures: £126,000 General Fund saving in 2028/29; £1,575,746 per annum programme value; 2026-29 grant cycle
findings.quote: In-year savings to the grants programme have never been proposed before.

findings.quote: Delivery of forecast savings is slower than anticipated

findings.paper_title: 4b.Appendix 2 - Children and Young People Select Committee proformas

findings.matters: Agency spend and recruitment delays are a common cost pressure, and this shows how one council plans to address them through a dedicated recruitment role.
findings.figures: agency controls saving £0.29m in 2027/28

findings.paper_title: 4b.Appendix 2 - Children and Young People Select Committee proformas

findings.detail: The paper says actuals for 2025/26 and 2026/27 and forecasts for 2027/28 and 2028/29 show these allocations are not needed in the directorate. The sums would go back to corporate budgets either in-year or in future years. The total saving is £5.36m in 2027/28 and £5.93m in 2028/29 when combined with other elements.
findings.matters: A directorate handing back held inflation allocations, rather than spending them, is a budget-setting move a finance director can compare with how their own corporately held inflation provisions are used.

findings.quote: these sums can be released back to corporate budgets either in-year or in future years

findings.matters: A residential placement pressure that is deferred to a later year rests on an assumed fall in numbers, which a finance director at this council or a peer can use to test a similar deferral.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension fund membership continues to mature with pensioner numbers growing while contributor numbers remain static
findings.detail: Active members remained stable at 6,737 (2025-26 vs 6,728 prior year) while pensioner numbers grew from 8,996 to 9,338 (+342, +3.8% year-on-year). Deferred members increased to 12,044. The admin team (10.4 FTE) now serves 2,704 members per staff member, up from 2,903 in the prior year, indicating increasing transaction complexity.
findings.matters: A maturing pension fund requires higher annual benefit payments relative to contributions, eventually necessitating asset liquidation rather than cash flow from new contributions. This structural change will increasingly pressure funding, even after the current surplus is achieved.
findings.figures: Pensioners: 9,338 (2025-26) vs 8,996 (2024-25), +3.8%; Active members: 6,737 stable; Deferred: 12,044 stable; Total membership: 28,119; Ratio: 2,704 members per 1 FTE (2025-26) vs 2,903 (2024-25)
findings.quote: the Membership of the Fund continues to mature and amidst a prolonged period of higher inflation, both of which increase the Fund's liabilities

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Investment strategy updated to allocate 1-3% of assets to local investment in LCIV pooling area
findings.detail: The revised Investment Strategy Statement (March 2026) introduced a new local investment framework aligned with government policy, setting a target allocation of 1-3% of total fund assets (£20-60m based on current size) for investments in the LCIV pooling area to support sustainable economic development.
findings.matters: Local investment mandates can increase governance complexity and may create conflicts between fiduciary duty (maximum returns) and policy objectives (supporting local economy). This commitment creates future reporting and monitoring obligations and constrains flexibility in asset allocation.
findings.figures: Local investment target: 1-3% of total assets (approximately £20-60m); LCIV pooling area footprint covers 33 London local authorities
findings.quote: A target allocation of between 1-3% of total assets is set aside for this purpose. LCIV will play a central role in identifying, monitoring, and stewarding these investments, ensuring that they deliver both financial returns and broader community benefits.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension administration expenses reduced 22.4% to £1.076m year-on-year
findings.detail: Administration expenses fell from £1.387m to £1.076m (down £311k), and total fund expenses (administration, oversight, and investment management) fell 15.0% from £3.870m to £3.287m. Investment management fees rose 10.1% to £1.598m, likely reflecting the transition to LCIV and increased passive fund costs.
findings.matters: Expense reductions improve net returns to the fund. However, the rise in investment management fees may indicate that pooling cost savings have not yet materialised, and per-member administration unit costs remain high at £169 per active member, £27 per deferred, £17 per pensioner.
findings.figures: Admin expenses £1,076k (2025-26) vs £1,387k (2024-25), down 22.4%; Total expenses £3,287k vs £3,870k, down 15.0%; Management fees £1,598k vs £1,452k, up 10.1%
findings.quote: Administration Expenses 1,076 1,387 (311) -22.4% ... Total Expenses 3,287 3,870 (582) -15.0%

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: 100% of fund assets transitioned to London CIV pooled arrangements by 31 March 2026 deadline
findings.detail: The council completed its compliance with the government's mandatory asset pooling requirement by moving all assets to the London Collective Investment Vehicle. An Investment Management Agreement was executed delegating implementation responsibility to LCIV while the council retains fiduciary duties including setting strategic asset allocation. This marks completion of a major structural transformation.
findings.matters: Achieving the government pooling deadline on time removes regulatory compliance risk. Pooling was expected to deliver cost efficiencies through scale, though the transition introduced reliance on a single primary manager and some uncertainty around transition costs.
findings.figures: 100% of assets in LCIV by 31 March 2026; 33 London authorities now shareholders in LCIV
findings.quote: By the end of March 2026, the Fund had transitioned 100% of its assets to the London CIV (LCIV), achieving full compliance with national pooling requirements and aligning with the broader policy objective of consolidating LGPS assets into larger, FCA-regulated investment pools.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Fund assets grew £155m (8.3%) to £2.036bn in year ending 31 March 2026, but continue to face headwinds from maturing membership
findings.detail: The fund increased its total value from £1.881bn to £2.036bn. However, the fund continues to mature with increasing pensioner numbers relative to contributors, and prolonged higher inflation increases liabilities. The annualised investment return over 12 months was 9.45%, marginally below the benchmark of 10.39%.
findings.matters: While strong asset growth is positive, the demographic shift (more pensioners, fewer contributors) means the fund will increasingly need income-producing assets rather than growth assets to meet current liabilities, constraining future return prospects.
findings.figures: £155m growth (8.3%); fund value £2.036bn; investment return 9.45% vs benchmark 10.39%; 5-year absolute return 5.79% vs benchmark 5.65%
findings.quote: The Fund has achieved positive results over the past year, increasing its value by £155m (8.3%), from £1.881bn to £2.036bn for its members. However, this growth has occurred as the Membership of the Fund continues to mature and amidst a prolonged period of higher inflation, both of which increase the Fund's liabilities.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's pension contribution rate reduced from 21.5% to 17.6% of pay from April 2026
findings.detail: Following the improved funding position, the actuary recommended lower employer contribution rates. The council's rate is falling by 3.9 percentage points. The funding plan has an 85% likelihood of success, though there remains a risk that contributions may need to increase at the next valuation in 2028.
findings.matters: This is a direct saving to the council's revenue budget. For every £1m of pensionable pay, the council saves approximately £39,000 annually compared to the previous rate, freeing resources for other services.
findings.figures: 21.5% (2025-26) to 17.6% (2026-27 onwards); 3.9 percentage point reduction; 85% likelihood of success
findings.quote: For the Council, a total contribution rate of 17.6% of pay is proposed, reflecting a primary rate of 19.8% and a secondary adjustment of -2.2%. findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Pension fund deficit closed and reversed to 19% surplus between 2022 and 2025 valuations
findings.detail: The triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 shows the Fund now 119% funded (£301m surplus), compared to 97% at the previous 2022 valuation. This improvement was primarily driven by higher discount rates (increased from 3.6% to 5.3% per annum) and favourable changes in financial assumptions.
findings.matters: Closing a pension fund deficit directly improves the council's finances and removes a significant long-term liability. The move to surplus also unlocks scope for lower employer contributions, reducing annual budget pressure.
findings.figures: 119% funded (2025) vs 97% (2022); £301m surplus; assets £1.88bn, liabilities £1.58bn; discount rate increased from 3.6% to 5.3% per annum
findings.quote: The Fund's triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025 confirms a significantly improved funding position, with the Fund now 119% funded, compared to 97% at the 2022 valuation. This represents a surplus of £301m, with assets of £1.88bn exceeding liabilities of £1.58bn.

findings.detail: Emergency repairs perform well at 96%, above London median of 95%. Non-emergency repairs lag significantly at 66%, 20 points below London median. Total Mobile introduction November 2025 improving visibility; council undertaking work on data quality around work closure dates. Performance gap indicates ongoing operational challenges in repairs delivery.
findings.matters: Significant performance gap versus peer median indicates service quality problem affecting tenant satisfaction and regulatory compliance
findings.figures: Non-emergency 66% on time 2025-26; London median 86%; emergency repairs 96% vs 95% median
findings.quote: In contrast, 66% of non-emergency responsive repairs were completed on time in 2025-26, below the London median of 86%.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Disrepair cases account for 36% of repair costs in 2025-26, described as placing "huge burden" on HRA and diverting funds from planned investment
findings.detail: Council notes considerable strain on HRA from pressure to invest in stock improvements while maintaining balance amid inflation and new regulations (fire, building safety, Awaab's Law). Disrepair case costs have risen significantly and now account for 36% of overall repair costs in 2025-26, diverting resources from planned and programmed works. Stock condition survey findings not yet fully modeled into HRA, expected to require additional resources.
findings.matters: HRA financial pressure from unplanned disrepair spending constrains capital investment and threatens medium-term debt sustainability
findings.figures: Disrepair at 36% of repair costs in 2025-26, significant increase from prior years; additional investment required for full survey integration
findings.quote: Disrepair is placing a huge burden on the HRA, diverting funds away from planned investment and programmed work, whether delivered by its Direct Labour Organisation and/or contractors.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Repairs work in progress reduced 42% year-on-year to 4,840 jobs
findings.detail: Repairs backlog fell from 8,359 jobs (March 2025) to 4,840 jobs (March 2026), driven by sustained efforts from Direct Labour Organisation and contractors. Of remaining jobs, 28% allocated to contractors and 72% to DLO. Total Mobile system introduced November 2025 improved visibility and control. Data cleansing increased confidence that remaining jobs reflect true outstanding work.
findings.matters: Significant operational progress on a major improvement area supports recovery narrative and addresses self-referral concern
findings.figures: 4,840 jobs March 2026 vs 8,359 March 2025 (42% reduction); 28% contractor allocation, 72% DLO
findings.quote: As at March 2026, repairs work in progress (WIP) stood at 4,840 jobs, representing a significant reduction from 8,359 jobs in March 2025.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Fire remedial actions backlog stalled at 2,466 overdue, ending momentum from prior year reduction
findings.detail: Backlog had reduced from over 5,000 at self-referral to 2,248 by end 2024-25. Progress halted during 2025-26 with numbers fluctuating between 2,214-2,494 and ending 2,466 in March 2026. Council confirms zero overdue immediate-risk (P1X) actions as of March 2026, meaning highest-risk fire safety issues addressed. Weekly monitoring in place but further work required for sustained reduction.
findings.matters: Building safety backlog plateau indicates execution risk and signals unresolved regulatory concern from March 2024 self-referral
findings.figures: 2,466 overdue March 2026; down from 5,000+ at self-referral; zero overdue P1X actions
findings.quote: Progress plateaued during 2025-26, with the number of overdue actions fluctuating between 2,214 and 2,494 throughout the year and ending at 2,466 in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Decent Homes Standard at 15.1% overall, exceeding council's target of 10% by March 2026
findings.detail: Overall non-decent homes improved from 17.4% in 2024-25 to 15.1% in 2025-26, representing material progress. However, this exceeded the council's March 2026 target of 10%. Performance reached approximately 12% in January 2026 but was affected by delays to major works programmes. The majority of failures are due to key building components reaching end of lifespan, outpacing replacement programmes.
findings.matters: Missing the Decent Homes target indicates slower execution than planned on a key regulatory issue from the March 2024 self-referral
findings.figures: 15.1% in 2025-26 vs 10% target; improved from 17.4% in 2024-25; represents 1,804 non-decent properties
findings.quote: the proportion of homes that do not meet the Decent Homes Standard reduced from 17.4% in 2024-25 to 15.1% in 2025-26. While this represents positive progress, it is above the council's target of 10% by March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Comprehensive stock survey found 26% of council-managed homes non-decent, higher than prior estimates
findings.detail: Prior estimates were based on a partial 2019 survey with extrapolated data. A comprehensive stock condition survey by Savills in early 2025 revealed 26% of council-managed homes non-decent. This higher-than-expected finding indicates substantially greater capital investment needs than previously modeled. Subsequent reduction to 16.1% by 2025-26 through targeted investment shows progress but starting point created significant HRA implications.
findings.matters: The survey revealed much larger than previously understood stock quality issues, increasing capital investment needs and HRA financial pressure
findings.figures: 26% of council-managed homes non-decent at survey; prior estimate ~17% based on 2019 partial survey; improved to 16.1% by 2025-26
findings.quote: The survey found that 26% of council-managed homes did not meet the Decent Homes Standard.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Council Housing Performance Overview 2025-26 REPORT
findings.headline: Council subject to Regulatory Notice from Regulator of Social Housing issued March 2024
findings.detail: The council self-referred to the Regulator in December 2023 regarding homes not meeting Decent Homes Standard, overdue fire remedial actions, and works in progress in Repairs Service. A regulatory notice was served in March 2024, and the council has been meeting monthly with the Regulator to provide progress updates on its Housing Improvement Plan.
findings.matters: Regulatory action signals governance failure and control issues, creating credit and reputational risk for lenders
findings.figures: Issued March 2024; monthly regulator engagement ongoing
findings.quote: Mayor and Cabinet should note that the council remains subject to a Regulatory Notice issued by the Regulator of Social Housing in March 2024.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Nightly paid temporary accommodation fell to 869 in July 2026, down from 1,512 in August 2024, a 43% reduction
findings.detail: Monitoring data shows the number of people in nightly paid temporary accommodation has declined substantially from a peak of 1,512 in August 2024 to 869 by July 2026, a reduction of 643 people. This 43% decrease in the homelessness caseload is significant for spending control, as temporary accommodation is high-cost. The related £2.49m Temporary Accommodation Cost Reduction saving is marked Green for delivery, and the reduced caseload demonstrates that this saving should be achievable.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is expensive; declining numbers free up budget headroom and reduce a service where spending can spiral; this is one of the few demand trends shown moving in a cost-reducing direction, supporting budget recovery.
findings.figures: 1,512 (August 2024 peak), 869 (July 2026), 643-person reduction (42.5%); £2.49m Temporary Accommodation Cost Reduction saving (Green status)
findings.quote: the level has increased from 1214 in April 2024 to a high of 1512 in August 2024, this has now reduced to 869 in July 2026.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Children with Education, Health Care Plans showing sustained upward trend across 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27
findings.detail: The monitoring dashboard includes a graph tracking EHCP numbers across three financial years. The visual shows the 2024-25 baseline line, the 2025-26 line positioned above it, and the 2026-27 line tracking above both prior years, indicating continued year-on-year growth. The graph shows numbers ranging from approximately 3,300 to 4,100 across the three-year period.
findings.matters: EHCP numbers drive significant and growing education, health, and social care spending; councils must forecast these costs over multiple years; sustained upward trends signal structural service pressures.
findings.figures: Approximately 3,300–4,100 range across three financial years with year-on-year increases visible
findings.quote: Children with Education, Health Care Plans

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Adult social care demand increased to 4,088 people supported by July 2026, up from 3,969 in April, a 3% rise in three months
findings.detail: Monitoring data shows the number of adults receiving social care rising from 3,969 in April to 4,088 in July, an increase of 119 people. This 3% growth in demand occurs against a backdrop of two major social care cost-control savings marked as at-risk: a £2.00m saving on Prevention & Technology improvements (Red) and a £0.50m saving from review of high-cost care home placements (Amber). Rising demand without achieved cost controls amplifies budget pressure.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a budget-critical service with structural demand growth; finance directors and lenders monitor demand trends closely, especially when planned cost controls are not materializing.
findings.figures: 4,088 (July), 3,969 (April), +119 people, +3% over three months
findings.quote: This graph shows the number of adults supported from 24/25 onwards. The source data is the Controcc System.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring Appendix
findings.headline: Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving £6.29m marked Red; Adult Social Care Prevention & Technology £2.00m and other Red items total £9.19m
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget savings plan includes multiple items marked Red (not on track) or Amber (at risk). The largest single Red item is Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving at £6.29m. Other Red-status items include Adult Social Care Prevention & Technology (£2.00m), Home School Transport (£0.40m), and Parking Contract (£0.50m). Amber items include Target Operating Model Review (£1.60m) and Care Home Placements review (£0.50m). Combined Red items total £9.19m, Amber items total £2.10m.
findings.matters: Local authorities must deliver planned savings to balance budgets; this level of at-risk savings—approximately 37% of the total plan—represents a significant threat to the 2026-27 financial position.
findings.figures: £6.29m (Placement Sufficiency), £2.00m (Adult Social Care Prevention), £1.60m (Target Operating Model Review), £0.50m (two items), £0.40m (Home School Transport); total Red £9.19m, total Amber £2.10m
findings.quote: Placement Sufficiency Cost Saving 6.29Red

findings.paper_title: Developing a Community-Led Housing Partnership Strategy REPORT v2
findings.headline: Council states financial constraints have made transfer of council land at below-market or nil value increasingly difficult; introduces 50% social rent threshold for land subsidies.
findings.detail: Council explicitly states it is 'operating within a challenging financial environment' which has made 'the Council's ability to support Community-Led Housing organisations through the transfer of land at below-market or nil value has become increasingly constrained'. However, it remains 'prepared to consider the transfer of land at below-market or nil value where a scheme can demonstrate a proportion of social rent delivery, at 50% or higher assessed against the social value generated', signalling a shift from unconditional land subsidy to conditional support tied to social outcomes.
findings.matters: Shows how financial constraints are reshaping council affordable housing policy and signals to lenders and peers how councils are tightening discretionary spending on asset transfers while maintaining strategic housing commitments.
findings.figures: 50% or higher social rent threshold for land transfers
findings.quote: Like many local authorities, the Council is operating within a challenging financial environment and must ensure that the use and disposal of public assets delivers the greatest possible benefit for residents. The Council's ability to support Community-Led Housing organisations through the transfer of land at below-market or nil value has become increasingly constrained

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Capital contingency allocation reduced from £10m to £3.2m after £4.4m drawdown for Town Centre and £1m commitment for Catford within four months
findings.detail: Full Council approved a £10m capital contingency allocation in July 2026 across General Fund and Housing Revenue Account budgets, funded from reserves. This report proposes to utilise £4.4m for the Town Centre Improvement Programme. An additional £1m capital budget was committed to the Catford Business Plan in September 2026. This leaves approximately £3.2m of the original £10m contingency remaining available.
findings.matters: Material drawdown of the capital contingency within four months reduces the council's financial flexibility for managing unforeseen events or capital pressures elsewhere. The remaining £3.2m headroom is modest relative to the council's overall capital programme exposure.
findings.figures: Total approved contingency July 2026: £10,000,000; Town Centre allocation: £4,403,053.70; Catford allocation September 2026: £1,000,000; remaining balance: approximately £3,200,000
findings.quote: This report is proposing to utilise £4.4m of this, which is in addition to the recent Catford Business Plan request in September which had agreement for £1.4m of revenue and £1m of capital budget, meaning that £3.2m will remain available.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Blue Garage Ltd awarded Library Operator concession contract for £10.7m over 10 years; operator income forecast £3.6m
findings.detail: Blue Garage Ltd selected after competitive procurement (two bids received, one failed quality threshold). The concession contract provides an initial 5-year term with council option to extend for further 5 years. Estimated contract value comprises £3.6m potential operator income plus £1.75m council fees over the initial 5-year period, totalling £5.35m per 5 years or £10.7m if fully extended. The original Mayor and Cabinet approval in September 2025 did not fully account for the concession value and VAT, necessitating this report to obtain approval of the correct contract value.
findings.matters: The concession model places operating revenue risk on the council. The operator must generate the forecasted £3.6m income or council's library service budget will be impacted. This contract structure is unusual for local government and requires effective performance management.
findings.figures: Estimated concession contract value 10 years £10,704,000; estimated operator income 5 years £3,600,000; estimated council fees 5 years £1,752,000
findings.quote: Approve the award of the Lewisham Library Operator concession contract to Blue Garage Ltd for a period of five years with the option to extend for up to a further 5 years at a value of £10,704,000 over the full contract period.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Programme completion funded through borrowing-backed capital headroom, carrying borrowing-cost and revenue implications not yet quantified in Part 1
findings.detail: The proposed funding route relies on borrowing to bridge the £4.5m additional requirement. The paper acknowledges this will carry borrowing-cost and revenue implications affecting the council's medium-term budget, but these financial impacts are not quantified in this Part 1 report.
findings.matters: Borrowing creates ongoing revenue budget impacts through interest and financing charges. The unquantified cost and the reduction in future capital flexibility are material considerations for the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Implied borrowing requirement approximately £4.5m; interest cost not quantified
findings.quote: The proposed funding route will rely on borrowing-backed capital headroom and will therefore carry borrowing-cost and revenue implications.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Market Canopy open procurement returned no compliant bids; FM Conway contract variation approved at £2.9m against original £1.6m design envelope
findings.detail: An open market procurement undertaken in 2025 received three tenders but none met the council's required quality threshold and submissions performed poorly on social value assessment. The council developed an alternative delivery route through FM Conway, its existing Highways Term Contractor, with Mayor and Cabinet approving a £2.9m contract variation in February 2026. This represents a £1.3m increase in this programme element alone compared to the original design procurement envelope of approximately £1.6m.
findings.matters: Procurement challenges forced a shift from open market competition to existing contractor arrangement. This element alone demonstrates the scale of construction cost pressure affecting the wider programme independent of the later Library discoveries.
findings.figures: Original procurement envelope approximately £1.6m; FM Conway approved variation £2.9m; increase £1.3m
findings.quote: Officers developed a delivery route through the Council's existing Highways Term Contractor, FM Conway, and Mayor and Cabinet approved a contract variation of £2.9m for that work in February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Library refurbishment discovered extensive concealed structural and building-fabric defects during construction, extending programme by almost a year
findings.detail: Rooff Construction commenced work on-site in September 2025. Opening-up of the building exposed significant defects including untied and unsafe brickwork requiring replacement with steel structures, corroded concrete reinforcement with exposed rebar, defective floor and roof structures, unsafe plantroom structure requiring demolition and replacement, and extensive additional fire safety works. The remedial works will extend the construction period by almost a year. Main Library construction is now forecast to complete summer 2027 with reopening in autumn 2027. Project reporting indicates positive contractor performance.
findings.matters: Hidden condition defects discovered in construction represent significant project delivery risk. The building was known to be complex pre-tender, but the extent of concealed structural and fabric issues could only be confirmed through intrusive opening-up works.
findings.figures: Original estimate approximately £5.4m; tender award £6,532,085; programme extension almost 12 months
findings.quote: Opening-up of the building then exposed further structural and building-fabric defects requiring significant remedial work and an extension of the construction programme.

findings.paper_title: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme – Programme and Budget Update PART 1
findings.headline: Lewisham Town Centre Improvement Programme funding requirement increased by £4.5m to £30.5m; £4.4m funded from capital contingency with remainder dependent on uncertain asset sale receipt
findings.detail: The programme's original budget was approximately £24m (£19m government grant plus £5m council match). The current additional requirement of £4.5m is being funded through an increased capital receipt estimate (£103k), drawing £4.4m from the capital contingency allocation approved in July 2026, and sale of site materials (£24k). The Library Resource Centre sale is estimated at £1.3m but is flagged as at-risk, with potential for receipts to be higher or lower. The updated total programme budget is now £30,488,326.
findings.matters: A 27% increase in programme cost is material and impacts the council's financial capacity and future capital planning. The funding route relies heavily on capital reserves and an uncertain asset sale, reducing flexibility for other capital priorities.
findings.figures: Original budget approximately £24m; additional requirement £4.5m; updated budget £30,488,326.00; contingency allocation £4,403,053.70; Library Resource Centre sale estimate £1,300,000
findings.quote: The current working additional funding requirement to complete LTCIP is around £4.5m, subject to final Finance reconciliation.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Strategy intended to improve value for money through competition and benchmarking; savings have not been quantified and no saving assumption built into HRA business plan
findings.detail: The strategy aims to improve value for money through competition, benchmarking, whole-life cost assessment and independent cost assurance. However, savings have not been quantified at this stage and no assumption of saving has been built into the HRA business plan. This is noted explicitly in financial implications.
findings.matters: For a £350m five-year programme, the expected value improvements and cost benefits of the procurement investment have not been quantified
findings.figures: £350m over five years to 2031; £70m annual programme
findings.quote: Savings have not been quantified at this stage and no assumption of saving has been built into the HRA business plan.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Framework vehicle choice determines whether procurement and management costs fall to HRA revenue or are capitalised through capital programme
findings.detail: A Lewisham-led framework carries procurement, legal and management costs that may fall to HRA revenue budgets. An external framework charges fees as a percentage of call-off value, potentially capitalisable. The options appraisal will compare total costs and relative HRA revenue and capital impacts of each option before authority to procure.
findings.matters: Framework choice affects both HRA revenue budget pressure and capital programme affordability in ways not yet quantified
findings.figures: External framework fees typically charged as percentage of call-off value
findings.quote: External framework fees are generally recovered through project expenditure and may therefore be capable of being capitalised as part of the cost of delivering works, whereas the procurement, legal and management costs associated with establishing a Lewisham-led framework may fall to HRA revenue budgets.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Additional client-side programme and contract-management capacity required; cost and HRA funding source to be quantified before authority to procure
findings.detail: A broader supplier base and stronger assurance model require additional client-side programme, commercial, technical and contract-management capacity. The council is explicitly told that the benefits in this report are not deliverable without that investment. The requirement will be quantified through a client capacity assessment before authority to procure.
findings.matters: Strategy cannot be delivered without resource investment whose scale, cost and HRA budget impact are not yet known
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Mayor and Cabinet is asked to note that the benefits set out in this report are not deliverable without that investment.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: New general major works arrangement must be mobilised by April 2028, well before existing contracts expire August 2029
findings.detail: The critical path requires authority to procure by April 2027, main competition during 2027, and mobilisation by April 2028—approximately 16 months before current contracts expire. The paper identifies procurement timetable slippage as a key risk, with escalation to Executive Management Team if mobilisation date is at risk.
findings.matters: Missing the April 2028 mobilisation target would leave only months before existing contracts expire, risking programme continuity and triggering contingency procurement costs
findings.figures: April 2028 required mobilisation; August 2029 contract expiry
findings.quote: The critical path is to obtain authority to procure by April 2027, complete the main competition during 2027 and mobilise the future general major works arrangement by April 2028, well before the current contracts expire in August 2029.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Independent reviews of major works schemes commissioned to examine scope and value for money; leaseholders have complained that estimated costs do not represent good value
findings.detail: The previous extension report identified programming gaps, variable delivery outcomes, and inconsistent contractor readiness. The council has commissioned independent reviews examining scope and value for money; findings are awaited. Leaseholders have separately complained that estimated costs from existing contracts do not represent good value.
findings.matters: Affordability and value-for-money concerns affect both operational performance and leaseholder service charge recovery, which are material to HRA revenue sustainability
findings.figures: £127m delivered by both contractors since 2021; reviews outcome awaited
findings.quote: There have also been leaseholder complaints that the estimated cost of works derived from the contracts do not represent good value.

findings.paper_title: Housing Major Works Procurement Strategy REPORT
findings.headline: Both measured term contracts can be terminated by either party with six months' notice; neither contract guarantees any volume of work
findings.detail: The council currently depends on United Infrastructure and Mulalley measured term contracts for major works. Both extend to August 2029 but carry no-fault break clauses exercisable by either party on six months' notice. The council is explicitly directed not to plan on the basis that both contracts will still be in place in 2029, creating immediate operational vulnerability.
findings.matters: For a £330m HRA capital programme over five years, unplanned loss of either contractor would create immediate delivery risk and require emergency replacement procurement
findings.figures: £70m annual programme; £330m HRA capital over five years to 2031; six months' termination notice; August 2029 expiry
findings.quote: Both MTCs carry a no-fault break provision on six months' notice, exercisable by either party, and neither guarantees any volume of work. The Council should therefore not plan on the basis that both contracts will run to August 2029.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Business Rates collected at 103% of 99% budgeted collection target as at 31 July
findings.detail: Business rates collection running ahead of target at 103% vs 99% budgeted collection rate. Collection described as 'higher than expected for this time of the year' due to school transfers of funds for payment. This represents positive performance in at least one revenue stream, offsetting council tax collection weakness.
findings.matters: Provides partial offset to council tax collection shortfall; shows resilience in at least one key revenue stream; demonstrates collection capability where economic conditions permit
findings.figures: 103% collection rate vs 99% target, £31.6m collected against £30.7m billed
findings.quote: £31.6m of business rates due had been collected which is a 103% collection rate, however, there is a budgeted 99% collection target

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Capital programme financing plan includes £294.1m prudential borrowing across MTFS period (£51.5m General Fund, £242.6m HRA)
findings.detail: Total capital programme £776.8m over MTFS period. 2026-27 allocation £244.0m with £36.0m (15%) spent to date by 31 July 2026. Prudential borrowing represents significant debt load across medium term. Financing also dependent on capital receipts, grants, and reserves. Some slippage evident: Strategic Regeneration Catford programme reduced from £2.2m budget to £0.7m forecast; some HRA projects under review. Revenue costs of financing will be material and dependent on interest rate environment.
findings.matters: Lenders need sight of total debt trajectory and affordability; HRA borrowing particularly material relative to declining reserves position; capital slippage affects treasury management and revenue cost management; interest rate risk on unfinanced borrowing
findings.figures: £294.1m prudential borrowing (£51.5m GF, £242.6m HRA), £776.8m total capital programme, £244.0m 2026-27 allocation, £36.0m spent (15%)
findings.quote: Total Prudential Borrowing of £294.1m across the MTFS period, of which £51.5m is for GF projects & £242.6m is for HRA projects.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Children's and Adult Social Care both forecasting £4.2m overspends driven by volume growth in placements, with £6.29m placement sufficiency saving rated Red
findings.detail: Children's Services: shift from in-house to external fostering agencies creating cost pressure; over-18s placement costs rising at rates higher than rest of London (no equivalent robust review has been conducted on over-18s as was done for under-18s); placement sufficiency saving of £6.29m is rated Red. Adult Social Care: forecast allows 'no headroom for additional growth'; packages and placements commitment increased £5.1m between 2025-26 outturn and current forecast; very high demand on hospital discharge pathway. Both services implementing oversight panels and cost management actions including recruitment restrictions, reablement focus, and AI assessment tools.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures in statutory services (Children Act and Care Act); no contingency for volume growth means any further increase will blow budget; cost management actions (panel oversight, recruitment restrictions) may impact service timeliness and quality; risks extend through year
findings.figures: Children's £4.2m overspend (Family Help & Care £4.7m), Adult Social Care £4.2m overspend, £5.1m increase in packages/placements, £6.29m placement sufficiency saving rated Red
findings.quote: There is an increase in those in external fostering agencies and reduction using in-house fostering which is causing a cost pressure. There is also an increase in costs related to those receiving care over 18 years old.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Parking Services contract delivering £1.3m overspend with additional £1.0m disputed claim from contractor Marston's for prior-year costs
findings.detail: Contract costs higher than anticipated. Contractor has claimed £1.0m for costs in previous financial year; claim rejected by council but contractor asserts debt remains outstanding and dispute is ongoing. Additional concern identified about ambiguity in debt management by contractor and whether council is assured it is receiving all income due.
findings.matters: Significant contract underperformance suggests either contract management weakness or unforeseen cost drivers; disputed liability creates contingent cash flow risk; wider debt collection assurance issue
findings.figures: £1.3m overspend, £1.0m disputed claim
findings.quote: The parking contractors, are claiming for costs of c£1m which were incurred in the previous financial year. These costs have been rejected, however, the company have stated that they believe that the debt is still outstanding.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: HRA closing reserves forecast at £14.0m, down from opening £45.9m, leaving only 'slightly above 10% recommended balance'
findings.detail: HRA reserves will be depleted by £31.9m through the year. £2.3m overspend combined with £25.0m planned revenue contribution to capital programme is driving drawdown (offset by capital financing transactions). Repairs & Maintenance showing £4.1m overspend due to disrepair project. Major works income is at risk: budgeted at £5.9m but 5-year average is £2.5m per annum, creating potential £3.4m shortfall. Minimal reserve buffer remaining after capital financing.
findings.matters: HRA reserve depletion significantly limits financial flexibility and leaves little buffer for unexpected pressures; raises questions about sustainability of capital programme financing model and adequacy of repair and maintenance management
findings.figures: £14.0m forecast closing, £45.9m opening, £31.9m drawdown, £2.3m overspend, £4.1m repairs overspend, £3.4m major works income at risk
findings.quote: It is currently forecast that reserves at the end of 2026/27 will be in the region of £14m, due to the planned financing of the capital programme, which would leave the closing balance only slightly above the 10% recommended balance to be held.

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Council Tax collection at 90% as at 31 July against 96% budgeted collection rate; £7.9m shortfall to be funded from reserves
findings.detail: Collection rate is 6 percentage points below target (90% actual vs 96% budgeted). This creates a £7.9m shortfall this year to be funded from collection fund reserves. Paper notes further 1% reduction in collection rates would cost the council £1.5m. Shortfall attributed to 'challenging economic times'. Depletion of collection fund reserves reduces future MTFS headroom and will require rebuilding.
findings.matters: Collection fund weakness erodes resources available this year and creates multi-year MTFS pressure to rebuild reserves; indicates economic stress in resident base and reduced collection resilience
findings.figures: 90% collected vs 96% target, £7.9m shortfall, £1.5m per 1% reduction
findings.quote: Collection rates for Council Tax may continue to be impacted due to the challenging economic times, especially if unemployment rises significantly

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: DSG High Needs Block forecasting £10.0m overspend; cumulative deficit projected at £34.0m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: Education, Health and Care Plan recipients have increased 259 in the past 12 months (from 3,744 to 4,003). High Needs Block overspend driven by both EHCP growth and provider cost uplifts. Cumulative DSG deficit at 31 March 2027 projected at £34.0m (up from £24.4m at 31 March 2026). Outcome of council's SEND Reform Plan submission (deadline June 2026) expected Autumn 2026; if successful could secure government funding of up to 90% of eligible deficit costs. If unsuccessful or unsupported, deficit falls to council within existing statutory override (extended to 31 March 2028).
findings.matters: Structural, growing pressure in special education spending; £34.0m deficit creates significant contingent liability dependent on autumn government decision; 24 schools already in deficit and facing additional 3.5% teaching and 3.3% support staff pay awards not fully funded
findings.figures: 259 EHCP increase (3,744 to 4,003), £10.0m overspend, £34.0m projected cumulative deficit at year-end, 90% potential government funding if SEND Plan successful
findings.quote: There are now 4,003 children with an EHCP compared to July 2025 with 3,744 children so an increase of 259 children in the 12 month period

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: Planned 2026-27 savings of £30.1m forecast to deliver only £20.4m; achievability down £7.7m since Period 2
findings.detail: Only 67.8% of budgeted savings are forecast to be achieved. Savings have become unachievable at scale: Children's placement sufficiency saving (£6.29m) and transport optimisation (£0.4m) are both rated Red; Adult Social Care budget review saving (£2.0m) is at risk with only £0.7m of mitigating actions identified. The £7.7m loss of achievability represents a major planning failure in just two months.
findings.matters: Savings shortfall compounds the overspend position and removes a planned lever for budget management; suggests budget setting assumptions were unrealistic or circumstances have changed materially
findings.figures: £30.07m planned savings, £20.38m forecast delivery, £7.69m loss of achievability, £6.29m placement saving at risk, £2.0m ASC saving at risk
findings.quote: currently £20.38m are anticipated to be achieved, this is a reduction of a achievable savings by £7.69m since Period 2

findings.paper_title: Financial Monitoring 2026-27 – Period 4 Monitoring REPORT
findings.headline: General Fund forecasting £7.0m overspend for 2026-27, up £3.9m since Period 2
findings.detail: Overspend of £7.0m represents 1.6% of the net budget of £424.8m. The position has deteriorated by £3.9m in the space of two reporting periods (May to July 2026). Main drivers are increased demand and costs in Children and Young People placements and transport (£2.7m movement), Adult Social Care placements (£1.5m), and parking contract costs (£1.3m).
findings.matters: Core revenue forecast is deteriorating in-year with no mitigation plan articulated; will require use of reserves or in-year corrective action to achieve budget balance
findings.figures: £7.0m overspend, £3.9m deterioration since Period 2, 1.6% of £424.8m net budget
