findings.paper_title: Approval to Extend the Council’s Insurances REPORT
findings.headline: Market conditions make new insurance procurement unlikely to achieve materially better pricing or terms than existing arrangements.
findings.detail: The council's appointed insurance brokers assessed market conditions and concluded that undertaking new procurement would not deliver better terms than the current arrangements. The public sector insurance market is served by a limited number of insurers, all experiencing inflationary and cost pressures. The council has decided to extend existing arrangements that have performed satisfactorily since 2023, maintaining relationship continuity and avoiding procurement costs.
findings.matters: Other councils considering whether to re-tender insurance arrangements need to understand whether competitive processes offer advantage in the current market environment.
findings.figures: Eight insurance lots covering all major classes; three-year initial contract from December 2023, now extended through November 2028.
findings.quote: market intelligence obtained through the Council's insurance brokers indicates that undertaking a new procurement exercise is unlikely to deliver materially better pricing or terms than those available under the existing arrangements.

findings.paper_title: Approval to Extend the Council’s Insurances REPORT
findings.headline: Insurance premiums have increased approximately 6% annually from 2023-2025, with similar increases expected during the 2026-2028 extension period.
findings.detail: Insurance costs rose from £2,392,171 in 2023 to £2,672,094 in 2025, representing roughly 6% annual increases. An indicative 6% increase from December 2026 would bring costs to £2,832,420 for the first year of extension. The two-year extension is budgeted at £5.8m. These increases reflect market-wide pressures affecting all public sector insurers, including inflation, litigation costs, property repair costs, and reinsurance expenses.
findings.matters: Finance directors need to understand fixed cost pressures that cannot be reduced through procurement due to universal market conditions, showing budget constraints extend even to unavoidable expenses.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Investment reserves declining from £264m to £210m as council depletes cash to fund capital, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.detail: The council's liquid investment portfolio has shrunk by £54m from £264m (June 2025) to £210m (June 2026), and the yield has fallen from 4.3% to 3.7%. The council is deliberately running down these reserves as an alternative to borrowing for capital spend, but this strategy is being exhausted. As cash reserves deplete, the council will become increasingly reliant on capital markets borrowing. The document indicates investment returns will continue to fall as interest rates are expected to decline.
findings.matters: Declining cash reserves indicate the council is exhausting alternative funding options and will become entirely dependent on borrowed funding once reserves are depleted, removing its financial buffer and making it more vulnerable to adverse borrowing conditions or unexpected cost pressures.
findings.figures: Investments: £264m (June 2025) → £210m (June 2026), a decline of £54m; yield declining from 4.3% to 3.7%.
findings.quote: The current investments of £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m 2025) will give the Council a 3.7% return compared to 4.3% at June 2025.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: LOBO loans reduced by £65m in two years (£119.7m to £54.3m), with further £17.5m repaid since April 2026, reducing refinancing risk.
findings.detail: The council has systematically reduced its LOBO (Lender's Option Borrower's Option) exposure from £119.7m to £54.3m over two years, plus an additional £17.5m repayment since April 2026. This brings the outstanding balance to approximately £36.8m. The council had been in correspondence with its LOBO lenders exploring rescheduling opportunities. This proactive reduction removes exposure to refinancing risk if lenders exercise their call option at higher rates.
findings.matters: LOBOs create refinancing risk at call dates; if exercised, the council must choose between repaying at par or accepting a new (potentially higher) rate. Reducing this exposure demonstrates sound risk management and reduces financial volatility from refinancing decisions outside the council's control.
findings.figures: LOBO loans: £119.7m (two years ago) → £54.3m (31 March 2026) → approximately £36.8m (post-April 2026); total reduction of £83m over two years.
findings.quote: In the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026. Since 1 April 2026 the Council has repaid a further £17.5m of LOBO loans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Debt service cost ratio rising from 4.8% to 7.7% of net revenue by 2027/28 (excluding PFI), reducing budget flexibility.
findings.detail: The proportion of revenue consumed by debt service is projected to increase from 4.8% (2025/26 actual) to 6.0% (2026/27) and 7.7% (2027/28), representing a 2.9 percentage point increase by 2027/28. This rising trend means an increasing share of the council's annual budget is locked into servicing debt, leaving less flexibility for service delivery and less resilience to unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: A rising debt service ratio indicates increasing financial stress and eroding budget flexibility. Lenders track this closely as an indicator of whether the council can sustain its debt burden without compromising service delivery or requiring spending cuts.
findings.figures: Financing costs as percentage of net revenue (excl. PFI): 4.8% (2025/26 actual), 6.0% (2026/27 estimate), 7.7% (2027/28 estimate).
findings.quote: This indicator identifies the trend in the cost of borrowing for capital purposes, against the net revenue stream.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 Council
findings.headline: Capital programme jumped 62% in three months from £421.4m to £684.6m, forcing substantial new borrowing (£72.6m in 2026/27 alone).
findings.detail: Between March and June 2026, Lewisham's four-year capital programme forecast increased by £263.2m — a 62% rise. This forces the council to shift from its under-borrowing strategy to active borrowing. The council will need £42m general fund borrowing and £30.6m HRA borrowing in 2026/27. The bulk of the increase comes from the Housing Revenue Account, particularly the 'Building for Lewisham' programme.
findings.matters: A lender would need to understand what is driving such a large and rapid increase in capital plans, whether this reflects a sustained policy shift, and how sustainable the resulting additional borrowing will be for the council's medium-term finances.
findings.figures: Capital programme: £421.4m (March 2026 forecast) to £684.6m (June 2026 forecast); prudential borrowing requirement: £42.0m general fund and £30.6m HRA for 2026/27.
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: Rate forecast already acknowledged as likely to be revised upward due to inflation pressures and unforeseen geopolitical events
findings.detail: The MUFG forecast was made in June 2026, before the ceasefire in the Middle East was broken. The council explicitly states it expects MUFG to provide a revised forecast as inflation pressures grow, indicating the current forecast may quickly become obsolete.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in financial projections; a council acknowledging that its rate forecast is likely to be revised upward within weeks suggests significant uncertainty about 2026-27 borrowing costs and the stability of treasury assumptions
findings.figures: Forecast made June 2026; Middle East conflict broke out after June; revision expected due to inflation
findings.quote: We expect MUFG to provide a revised forecast as pressure on inflation grows.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: Treasury advisor recommends borrowing at shorter end of curve rather than longer term due to expensive long-term PWLB rates
findings.detail: MUFG's borrowing advice states that all PWLB certainty rates are currently significantly above the neutral 3.5% Bank Rate level. MUFG advises better value can be obtained at the shorter end of the curve and short-dated fixed Local Authority to Local Authority monies should be considered, rather than longer-maturity borrowing.
findings.matters: The advisor is flagging that long-term borrowing is currently expensive relative to long-term neutral levels; councils considering capital expenditure will face higher costs if borrowing long-term
findings.figures: MUFG neutral Bank Rate forecast 3.5% (long-term); all PWLB certainty rates currently significantly above this level
findings.quote: Overall, better value can be obtained at the shorter end of the curve and short-dated fixed LA to LA monies should also be considered.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: UK inflation remains stubborn with risk of breaching 4.5%, driving expectations of higher debt interest costs
findings.detail: UK inflation peaked at 3.8% then dipped to 3% in January-February before core inflation rose to 3.2% in February. The document warns that recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later in 2026. This inflation backdrop is expected to increase government debt interest repayments by approximately £10bn.
findings.matters: Rising inflation increases the cost to a council of servicing existing and new debt, and indicates a risk that council spending pressures (utilities, energy costs) will also rise
findings.figures: CPI peaked at 3.8%, dipped to 3%, core inflation 3.2% in February; risk of breaching 4.5% later in year; government debt interest repayment increase of £10bn
findings.quote: the recent upward pressure on energy costs could see CPI inflation breach 4.5% later this year.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Strategy 2026-27 Appendices - Final
findings.headline: Interest rate forecast shifted to expect Bank Rate will remain at 3.75% or rise, not fall, as inflation pressures increase
findings.detail: MUFG Corporate Markets now expects the MPC will not cut Bank Rate and may even raise rates due to inflation driven by the war in the Middle East. The forecast was made in June 2026 before the ceasefire was broken. This represents a shift from earlier expectations of rate cuts. The PWLB borrowing rates forecast shows 5-year rates at 4.30% in September 2026, 10-year at 4.90%, and 25-year at 5.60%.
findings.matters: If Bank Rate remains at 3.75% or rises rather than falls, councils face higher borrowing costs for 2026-27; this affects both the cost of any new borrowing and the calculus on refinancing existing debt
findings.figures: Bank Rate forecast 3.75% (Sep 2026-Sep 2027); PWLB rates 5-year 4.30%, 10-year 4.90%, 25-year 5.60%
findings.quote: MUFG Corporate Markets now expect the MPC will not cut Bank Rate and may even raise rates as inflation increases due to the war in the Middle East.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Fund administration staffed by 10.4 FTE managing 28,119 members, an increasing workload pressure despite improving efficiency metrics.
findings.detail: The 10.4 FTE pension team serves approximately 28,000 members across the council, scheduled bodies and admitted bodies. The ratio has improved from 2,903 members per FTE (2024/25) to 2,704 per FTE (2025/26). However, the paper shows this team is also doing non-pension work including redundancy calculations and LPFA/TPA data provision, suggesting stretched capacity.
findings.matters: A small team managing a large, complex membership with growing transaction volumes increases risk of error and service failure. The paper hints at this through the internal audit findings on payment accuracy. Staffing constraints could affect the council's ability to respond to regulatory changes or member queries.
findings.figures: 10.4 FTE; 28,119 members; ratio 2,704 members per FTE; 1,197 transactions per staff member per year
findings.quote: the role of the pensions section in the administering authority during 2025/26 was carried out by 10.4 Full Time Equivalent (FTE) staff serving some 28,000 members.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 3. Pension Fund Draft Annual Report 2025-26
findings.headline: Council's pension contribution rate cut from 21.5% to 17.6% from April 2026, releasing budget headroom.
findings.detail: The 2025 triennial valuation showed the fund improved to 119% funded (from 97% in 2022) with a £301m surplus. The actuary recommended lower employer contribution rates. For Lewisham Council specifically, the contribution rate falls from 21.5% to 17.6% of pensionable pay from 1 April 2026.
findings.matters: This is a material cost reduction for the council's budget, freeing up resources for other pressures. A lender would see this as either improving financial flexibility or flag it as a one-off benefit that may not recur.
findings.figures: 21.5% reducing to 17.6% from 1 April 2026; surplus £301m; 119% funded vs 97% in 2022
findings.quote: This strengthened funding position enabled the Fund's actuary to recommend lower employer contribution rates from 1 April 2026, with the Council's contribution rate reducing from 21.5% to 17.6% of pensionable pay.

Sector faces pressure from 3.5% teaching staff and 3.3% support staff pay awards that will not be fully funded despite grant support. Central Schools Services Block has annual 20% reduction. Structural funding pressure evident.

findings.paper_title: 6. PASC P3 Monitoring Report Sep26
findings.headline: Financial forecast does not yet include transitional or policy costs from new administration elected May 2026

Forecast explicitly excludes once-off transition costs (assumed to fund from corporate provisions) and any pressures from new policies that cannot fit within existing budget. Any new priorities requiring additional spending would be reported as overspend.
findings.matters: Unquantified policy costs from new administration represent a contingent liability; could emerge as in-year pressures if they require spending above current envelope

findings.paper_title: 6. PASC P3 Monitoring Report Sep26
findings.headline: Capital programme £24.6m spent (10% of allocation) by end June; major schemes mobilising but Building Safety Act constraints remain
findings.detail: 2026/27 capital allocation £242.7m (£113.3m GF, £119.3m HRA). Spend to 30 June only £24.6m (10% of annual budget). Major schemes now mobilised: Catford Campus (major works starting), LUF Cultural Hub (Lewisham Library works begun), Building for Lewisham HRA (major projects on site). Spend delivery constrained by Building Safety Act requirements for high-rise works, affecting pace of mobilisation.

findings.paper_title: 6. PASC P3 Monitoring Report Sep26
findings.headline: Proposed pay award 3.3% rejected by unions; budgeted only 3%; London Living Wage commitments creating pressure
findings.detail: Council proposed 3.3% pay award for staff below Chief Executive level, rejected by unions. Budget assumed 3% salary inflation. Council committed to London Living Wage for all contracted services; historical increases have exceeded 3% assumption. General CPI at 2.6% (June 2026) against 3.0% budgeted. Multiple cost drivers (pay awards, living wage, CPI) trending above budget simultaneously.
findings.matters: Multiple employment cost drivers all exceeding budget assumptions create structural pressure affecting all councils with similar living wage commitments and unionised workforces
findings.figures: 3.3% pay award proposed vs 3.0% budgeted; CPI 2.6% (June 2026) vs 3.0% budgeted
findings.quote: The proposed pay awards for 2026/27 of 3.3% for all officers below the Chief Executive pay bands has been rejected by the unions, this already exceeds the salary inflation allowance of 3% budgeted for.

findings.paper_title: 6. PASC P3 Monitoring Report Sep26
findings.headline: Council tax collection at 91% of 96% budgeted target; business rates at 95% of 99% target; collection fund reserve depleting
findings.detail: Council tax: £56.3m collected of £61.9m billed (91%), creating £5.6m shortfall against 96% target. Business rates: £22.3m collected of £23.8m billed (94% of amount, 95% of 99% target). Shortfalls funded via Collection Fund Reserve drawdown rather than budget adjustment, meaning reserve is being depleted. Report identifies economic conditions as risk factor for future collection rates.
findings.matters: Collection fund reserve depletion means future years must rebuild reserves or absorb permanent revenue budget impact; trends of persistent shortfalls migrate from reserves to MTFS
findings.figures: Council tax: £56.3m collected vs £61.9m billed (91% vs 96% target); £5.6m shortfall. Business rates: £22.3m (95% of target vs 99%)
findings.quote: As at 30th June 2026, £61.9m of Council Tax has been billed, of which £56.3m has been collected, representing 91% of the amount required to meet the targeted 96% collection rate.

findings.figures: £1.3m Parking Services overspend; ~£1.0m contractor claim (disputed); £1.0m estimated risk

findings.detail: Overspend on packages and placements occurring despite £6.5m growth allocated in budget setting. findings.detail: Overspend up £1.9m from Period 2 (£1.8m to £3.7m), signalling accelerating demand pressure. Family Help and Care £4.2m overspend due to additional young people in residential care and increased costs for over-18s. Education Services £1.0m overspend from school transport; pupil numbers up 98 year-on-year (1,270 June 2026 vs 1,172 June 2025), with 80 added since March 2026. Five initiatives totalling £10.79m are flagged as at-risk: two marked Red (adult social care budget review £2.0m, home school transport £0.40m) and three marked Amber (placement sufficiency £6.29m, parking contract £0.50m, target operating model review £1.60m).

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Net borrowing requirement for 2025/26 was £9.7m, down from £60.8m in 2024/25
findings.detail: The net borrowing requirement fell significantly year-on-year from £60.8m to £9.7m, a reduction of £51.1m or 84%. This improvement reflects lower capital investment in the year (£137.1m vs £159.3m), higher capital grants received (£47.5m), increased capital receipts (£6.2m), and revenue contributions to capital expenditure (£18.6m). However, forward projections indicate this improvement will reverse due to the capital programme expansion and higher borrowing needs in 2026/27 and beyond.
findings.matters: Shows the underlying improvement in borrowing pressures for 2025/26; context for understanding that forward trajectory is now moving sharply higher.
findings.figures: Net borrowing requirement 2024/25: £60.8m; 2025/26: £9.7m; reduction of £51.1m or 84%
findings.quote: In respect of the net borrowing requirement for 2025/26 it was £9.7m, this being £51.1m lower than the net borrowing requirement of £60.8m for 2024/25

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Council forecast to require £72.6m of prudential borrowing in 2026/27: £42.0m general fund, £30.6m housing revenue account
findings.detail: To fund the capital programme, the council forecasts requiring £72.6m of new prudential borrowing in 2026/27. The general fund requires £42.0m and the housing revenue account requires £30.6m. This new external borrowing will add to the council's debt portfolio and increase future debt service costs. Over the 2026-30 period, cumulative prudential borrowing is forecast at £249.8m (general fund £51.6m, HRA £198.2m).
findings.matters: Indicates the scale of new external financing the council will need to raise in the near term and the resulting growth in the debt portfolio and future debt service obligations.
findings.figures: Prudential borrowing 2026/27: £42.0m general fund, £30.6m HRA, total £72.6m; cumulative 2026-30: £249.8m
findings.quote: The table below shows the required prudential borrowing required in 2026/27 which is £42.0m for the general fund and £30.6m for the HRA.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Internal borrowing increased to £345.4m as at 31 March 2026 from £328.8m previous year
findings.detail: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position, using reserves and cash balances to fund £345.4m of its £689.3m capital financing requirement, with the remainder (£343.9m) funded by external debt. This strategy is pursued while investment returns (3.7%) remain lower than borrowing costs. As the capital programme expands and investment balances decline, this internal borrowing gap is forecast to widen, requiring eventual recourse to external borrowing.
findings.matters: Shows the council's capital financing strategy and cash position; the growing gap between capital financing requirement and external debt signals increasing dependence on cash reserves as investments are drawn down.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £328.8m (2024/25) → £345.4m (2025/26); Capital Financing Requirement £689.3m; external debt £343.9m at 31 March 2026
findings.quote: As at 31 March 2026, this internal borrowing was £345.4m, which is the difference between the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR) and the Council's actual borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream forecast at 18.0% for 2026/27, up from 15.9% in 2025/26
findings.detail: The share of net revenue dedicated to servicing debt is forecast to increase by 1.1 percentage points in 2026/27. Excluding PFI costs (which are funded by government grants), the financing ratio rises from 4.8% to 6.0%. The increase reflects the combined effect of higher PWLB borrowing rates (forecast at 4.8-5.0% for 5-10 year loans) and the council's increased borrowing to fund the expanded capital programme.
findings.matters: Illustrates the growing share of revenue budget committed to debt service; shows the financial impact of higher interest rates and increased borrowing on the council's underlying affordability.
findings.figures: Financing costs ratio (including PFI) 15.9% (2025/26) → 18.0% (2026/27); excluding PFI 4.8% → 6.0%; PWLB rates forecast 4.8-5.0% for 5-10 year maturity
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs* to Net Revenue Stream 2025/26 Actual 15.9% 2026/27 Estimate 18.0%

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Investment portfolio fell from £264m to £210m year-on-year with annualised yield declining from 4.3% to 3.7%
findings.detail: The council's treasury investments declined by £54m in the year to 30 June 2026 and the yield on the portfolio fell from 4.3% to 3.7%. The council is using investment balances to fund capital expenditure rather than raising external borrowing, as returns on investment remain lower than borrowing costs. The paper forecasts continued decline in the investment portfolio during 2026/27 as the capital programme accelerates and new borrowing is drawn.
findings.matters: Shows the council is drawing on reserves to fund its expanded capital programme; declining investments reduce the income cushion and liquidity buffer available for operational flexibility.
findings.figures: Investments £264m (June 2025) → £210m (June 2026); yield 4.3% → 3.7%; investment income expected to continue falling during 2026/27
findings.quote: The current investments of £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m 2025) will give the Council a 3.7% return compared to 4.3% at June 2025. The investment balance will continue to fall during 2026/27 as the planned capital programme uses the some of the investment cash as well as taking on new borrowing.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: LOBO loans reduced from £119.7m to £54.3m over two years, with further £17.5m repaid in April-June 2026
findings.detail: The council has aggressively reduced its exposure to LOBO (Lender Option Borrower Option) loans, which carry refinancing risk when lenders exercise call options. From £119.7m two years prior, the portfolio was cut to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026, and an additional £17.5m was repaid between 1 April and 30 June 2026. The council engaged with LOBO lenders during 2024-2025 on rescheduling opportunities and continues to monitor the position if further calls occur.
findings.matters: Demonstrates deliberate action to reduce refinancing risk exposure where lenders hold the option to propose higher rates at call dates; shows active debt portfolio management.
findings.figures: LOBO loans reduced from £119.7m (two years ago) to £54.3m (31 March 2026); additional £17.5m repaid 1 April - 30 June 2026; £65.4m reduction over three-year period
findings.quote: In the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026. Since 1 April 2026 the Council has repaid a further £17.5m of LOBO loans.

findings.paper_title: 5a. Treasury Management Outturn and Mid Year Review 202627
findings.headline: Capital Programme for 2026-30 increased from £421.4m to £684.6m between March and June 2026
findings.detail: The capital programme was revised upward from £421.4m (agreed March 2026) to £684.6m (forecast June 2026), representing a 62% increase. The revised programme comprises general fund capital expenditure of £166.2m and housing revenue account spending of £508.4m across the 2026-30 period. The main components are building new housing (£219.7m) and HRA decent homes spending (£268.6m). This material increase in planned capital expenditure will drive substantially higher capital financing requirements and borrowing needs.
findings.matters: A material expansion in capital plans directly increases the council's underlying borrowing need and sets the scale of treasury and financing decisions for the period ahead.
findings.figures: Capital Programme £421.4m (March 2026) → £684.6m (June 2026), increase of £263.2m; general fund £166.2m, HRA £508.4m over 2026-30
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 PASC Cover
findings.headline: Council forecasts interest rates may fall later in 2026/27 if the Middle East conflict ends and inflation stabilises.
findings.detail: The paper provides an economic outlook noting that geopolitical events and inflation dynamics may shape interest rate movements. Lower rates later in the year could improve the cost of new borrowing and returns on investments, though this is conditional on external events.
findings.matters: Interest rate assumptions underpin treasury forecasts and borrowing decisions. This comment signals management is monitoring economic conditions and their impact on the funding cost of the expanded capital programme.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: If the conflict in the Middle East comes to an end, then interest rates may fall later in the year as inflation stabilises.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 PASC Cover
findings.headline: External borrowing decreased from £350.9m to £343.9m but the council has not breached operational or authorised borrowing limits.
findings.detail: Borrowing fell slightly year-on-year, indicating some repayment of existing debt. The council confirms its operational boundary and authorised limit have not been breached and forecasts no difficulty complying with the CIPFA Code's prudential borrowing requirements for current or future years.
findings.matters: The council is in headroom on its borrowing limits, which provides capacity to finance the expanded capital programme. For a lender, it confirms the council remains within regulatory prudential limits and is not in distress.
findings.figures: External borrowing £343.9m as at 31 March 2026 (£350.9m in 2025)
findings.quote: The total external borrowing for the Council was £343.9m as at 31 March 2026 (£350.9m 2025).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 PASC Cover
findings.headline: Investment balances fell from £264m to £210m and will continue to fall as planned capital programme draws on investment cash alongside new borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's investment holdings have declined by £54m (20%) year-on-year and the return on those investments has fallen from 4.3% to 3.7%. The council explicitly forecasts further drawdown of investment balances during 2026/27 to fund the capital programme alongside new borrowing.
findings.matters: Falling investment balances signal the council is consuming its liquid reserves to fund capital investment. This reduces financial flexibility and resilience; it is a pattern lenders and peer authorities monitor closely as it indicates how the council is managing the tension between capital ambitions and available cash.
findings.figures: Investments £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m in 2025); return 3.7% (4.3% in 2025)
findings.quote: The current investments of £210m as at 30 June 2026 (£264m 2025) will give the Council a 3.7% return compared to 4.3% at June 2025. The investment balance will continue to fall during 2026/27 as the planned capital programme uses the some of the investment cash as well as taking on new borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 PASC Cover
findings.headline: Capital Programme for 2026-30 increased from £421.4m to £684.6m between March and June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.
findings.detail: The council's capital investment plans expanded by 62% mid-year. The paper notes the expanded programme will be funded through a combination of investment drawdown and new borrowing, but does not break down the composition of the increase in this cover sheet.
findings.matters: A £263m mid-year expansion in capital plans directly affects borrowing requirements, cash management, and the council's forward financial position. Finance directors across local government and lenders track capital programme changes as indicators of strategic shift.

findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4. Catford Regeneration Programme Business Plan v.FINAL
findings.headline: Unfunded ongoing maintenance and enhanced project management capacity identified as necessary for delivery success, adding to capital and revenue funding pressures
findings.detail: Beyond capital gaps, the business plan identifies specific revenue pressures: ongoing maintenance costs and 'the need for enhanced programme/project management capacity.' Town centre management activity is mostly funded through existing budgets but 'physical capital works to support crime and ASB prevention are not funded.' The business plan emphasises that 'The resourcing challenges will need to be addressed for the programme to be delivered successfully,' yet identifies no funding source for these requirements.
findings.matters: Unfunded operational costs and management capacity often emerge as revenue pressures post-delivery; their explicit identification but non-funding signals risks to implementation quality and service delivery sustainability.
findings.figures: Enhanced project management capacity required but unfunded; physical crime prevention works not funded
findings.quote: Revenue pressures associated with project delivery, ongoing maintenance and the need for enhanced programme/project management capacity. The resourcing challenges will need to be addressed for the programme to be delivered successfully.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4. Catford Regeneration Programme Business Plan v.FINAL
findings.headline: Regeneration programme faces 'insufficient capital and revenue budgets' with identified funding gaps for High Street Place Lab and limited contingency allowances
findings.detail: The business plan explicitly states there is 'insufficient capital and revenue budgets available to deliver the entirety of the programme.' Capital funding gaps are specifically identified for the High Street Place Lab programme. Even where funding is secured for core transport projects, 'contingency allowances remain limited and aspects of the programme may need to be refined to remain within budget.' Limited funding is also available for wider activation programmes, cultural activity, and retrofit initiatives.
findings.matters: Explicit acknowledgment of insufficient budgets across a major regeneration programme signals either undelivered projects or potential unplanned calls on council reserves or borrowing.
findings.figures: Core transport projects (Station Links, A205/A21, Thomas Lane Yard) described as fully funded; High Street Place Lab programme and wider retrofit/activation programmes lack identified funding
findings.quote: Many of them faces ongoing financial pressures and delivery risks. These include capital funding gaps for delivery of project like the High Street Place Lab programme and revenue pressures associated with project delivery, ongoing maintenance.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 4. Catford Regeneration Programme Business Plan v.FINAL
findings.headline: Council's wholly owned company CRPL identified as central constraint to regeneration, with financial position limiting investment capability and requiring council mitigation
findings.detail: CRPL is the primary landowner in Catford town centre, holding Catford Shopping Centre, 22 commercial units, 17 residential properties and other assets. The business plan explicitly identifies 'Minimise and mitigate the council's financial exposure from CRPL' as a key programme outcome. The document states that CRPL's financial position limits its ability to invest, actively shape the town centre offer and support regeneration outcomes without council intervention.
findings.matters: A council-owned company's financial weakness that the council must actively manage represents a potential financial liability and affects the council's flexibility to deploy capital elsewhere.
findings.figures: CRPL portfolio: 22 commercial units in shopping centre, 9 on Broadway, 17 residential properties, The Catford House, Brookdale Club, 9 Holbeach Road
findings.quote: This position limits the company's ability to invest, actively shape the town centre offer and support regeneration outcomes without intervention from the Council.

findings.paper_title: Permission to Procure and Award Multiple Housing Revenue Works Contracts - Report
findings.headline: Leaseholder cost recovery subject to statutory section 20 consultation; failure to comply could cap charges at £250 and reduce HRA income
findings.detail: Where contracts include works with costs recoverable through leaseholder service charges, the council must comply with section 20 consultation requirements under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985. Failure to comply results in statutory cap on leaseholder cost recovery at £250 per leaseholder maximum, reducing budgeted HRA income. Council has built consultation into its procurement timeline (Oct 2026 and Feb 2027).
findings.matters: Leaseholder charges are a material HRA income stream; failure to follow proper consultation process could significantly reduce budgeted cost recovery and create unplanned financial pressure on HRA
findings.figures: Statutory cap at £250 per leaseholder if consultation requirements not met
findings.quote: Failure to comply with these requirements will result in potential capping of leasehold charges and lost income to the authority

findings.paper_title: Permission to Procure and Award Multiple Housing Revenue Works Contracts - Report
findings.headline: Council procuring £83m of housing works contracts over five years (3+1+1 term) with budget availability explicitly confirmed and no identified fund pressures
findings.detail: Council is procuring five lots of housing works contracts totalling £83m over five years (three-year term with two one-year extension options), with estimated annual spend of £16.6m. The paper explicitly confirms sufficient budget is available and the award will not present fund pressures.
findings.matters: Material five-year capital procurement indicates scale of execution risk; explicit confirmation of budget availability shows financial discipline and reduces the risk of funding gaps mid-contract
findings.figures: £83m total over 5 years; £16.6m annual spend; 3+1+1 contract term structure
findings.quote: Sufficient budget is available, and the award of these contracts will not present fund pressures

findings.paper_title: Permission to Procure and Award Multiple Housing Revenue Works Contracts - Report
findings.headline: Disrepair backlog and Awaab's Law compliance requirements driving procurement of five specialist contractor lots, including dedicated £7m damp and mould and £9m disrepair streams
findings.detail: Council has identified a backlog of disrepair work and faces increasing regulatory scrutiny from Awaab's Law (damp and mould requirements). The council logged approximately 70,000 repairs in 2024/2025. Lot 3 (£7m) and Lot 4 (£9m) specifically address damp/mould and disrepair compliance.
findings.matters: Regulatory compliance failures and repair backlogs create financial exposure and operational risk; how councils address these pressures affects their financial stability, asset condition, and exposure to legal challenge
findings.figures: c70,000 repairs logged 2024/2025; Lot 3 (Damp and Mould) £7m; Lot 4 (Disrepair) £9m
findings.quote: There is a backlog of disrepair work, and the ever-increasing scrutiny and requirements introduced by Awaab's Law will continue to lead to more complex challenges

findings.paper_title: Permission to Procure and Award Multiple Housing Revenue Works Contracts - Report
findings.headline: Five-year budget allocation of £451.7m for housing repairs and capital confirmed in February 2026 budget (£320.9m capital, £130.8m revenue)
findings.detail: Mayor & Cabinet budget report (February 2026) allocated £451.7m over five years from 2026/27 for HRA repairs and capital programs. This allocation will fund the costs of the contracts being procured. The council is now executing this planned investment.
findings.matters: Early, ringfenced allocation of repair and capital budgets demonstrates financial planning and signals priority investment in housing stock maintenance; relevant to understanding councils' financial commitments to asset condition
findings.figures: £451.7m total over 5 years; £320.9m capital; £130.8m revenue repairs
findings.quote: over a five-year period from 2026/27 a total of £451.7m, will be allocated to the Repairs and Capital programmes, broken down as £320.9m capital and £130.8m revenue Repairs

findings.paper_title: Permission to Procure and Award Multiple Housing Revenue Works Contracts - Report
findings.headline: Housing portfolio growing by approximately 2,000 units over two years, increasing maintenance service demands
findings.detail: Council's housing portfolio will grow by c2,000 units over the next two years. This growth contextualizes the need for the current procurement and increases the scale of future maintenance and repair services required from contractors.
findings.matters: Growing housing stock increases future maintenance and repair burdens; relevant to understanding the long-term operational and financial commitments required from councils managing expanding portfolios
findings.figures: c2,000 unit growth over two years
findings.quote: the homes managed by the housing service is set to increase as the housing portfolio grows by c2,000 over the next two years

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Service has undergone prior £350,000 reduction in 2021/22 and now spends less per capita than most comparable Inner London boroughs, despite serving a higher-deprivation population.
findings.detail: The service was subject to a £350,000 budget cut in 2021/22, which became the budget base for re-commissioning in 2022/23. Current per capita spend on 0-19 Public Health Nursing is moderate across all London boroughs, but when compared with Inner London boroughs only, Lewisham spends less per capita than most other areas. This is notable given that Lewisham has relatively high deprivation levels compared to other London boroughs. Efficiencies have been achieved through increased skill-mix and management restructuring.
findings.matters: Shows council has limited scope for further efficiency savings in this service; relevant for understanding constraints on spending and whether current service levels are sustainable relative to deprivation need.
findings.quote: A £350,000 cut was made to the contact value in the 2021/22 financial year.

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Funding cliff at 31 March 2029: variations to service (PAIRS and Specialist Nurse roles) end at this date, and core contract continuation depends on annual Public Health Grant allocation.
findings.detail: The Parent-Infant Relationship Services (PAIRS) variation is funded until 31 March 2029, with continuation beyond uncertain. The Specialist School Nurse for Integrated Adolescent Service is similarly funded only until 31 March 2029. The core contract extends to 31 March 2030, but funding comes from annual Public Health Grant allocation, which is subject to government spending decisions. Any uplift to contract value for NHS pay awards must be affordable within available grant allocations.
findings.matters: Creates requirement for council financial planning beyond 2029 to either secure grant continuation, find alternative funding, or plan service reductions; relevant to understanding future financial commitments and risks.
findings.figures: 31 March 2029 (end date for variation services); 31 March 2030 (end date for core contract)
findings.quote: Provision of the grant beyond this point is unknown.

findings.paper_title: Approval to enact permitted extension to 0-19 Public Health Nursing Service contract - Report
findings.headline: Service extension performs better than statistical neighbours and national average on most key performance indicators, supporting decision to extend existing provider rather than procure competitively.
findings.detail: The provider's performance data shows Lewisham Health Visiting Service exceeding statistical neighbours and national averages on most measures: 92% of families receiving new birth visit within 14 days (vs 86% nationally), 90% receiving 6-8 week review (vs 87% nationally), 84% receiving 1-year developmental review (vs 73% statistical neighbours), and 92% of 2-year-olds achieving expected development level (vs 83% nationally). Breastfeeding at 6-8 weeks is 85% vs 57% nationally. Recent commissioning of similar services across London shows minimal competing bids, making a new procurement unlikely to add value.
findings.matters: Demonstrates council is making evidence-based decisions about service continuity; relevant for other councils assessing whether to extend or re-tender established health services.
findings.quote: Based on recent commissioning of Health Visiting and School Nursing Services across London, and the previous commissioning of this contract, it is unlikely that any other NHS Trusts would compete with LGT to bid for the contract.

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Revenue savings from external placement cost avoidance are ring-fenced in reserve for capital and lifecycle costs, not available for general council budget.
findings.detail: Council proposes that cost savings from in-house placement versus external providers will be transferred to earmarked reserve. Reserve will first repay £479,000 additional capital investment, then fund ongoing capital, lifecycle and maintenance costs. This means the savings cannot be deployed to offset pressures elsewhere in council budget.
findings.matters: Ring-fencing of savings constrains council flexibility to redeploy resources for other budget pressures; the savings are non-cashable and dedicated to supporting Kirkdale's ongoing financial obligations.
findings.figures: £479,000 capital to be repaid from savings; Remaining savings transferred to reserve for capital and lifecycle costs
findings.quote: Agree that any early cost savings will first be used to repay the additional capital investment, referred to above, of £479,000 and that any further savings will be transferred to an earmarked reserve to support ongoing capital, lifecycle and maintenance costs

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Multiple financial assumptions underpinning sinking fund are at risk, potentially accelerating point at which corporate support required.
findings.detail: Model depends on: costs rising by 3% annually; external placement costs at £2.4m per year; occupancy at 90%; void rate at 10%. Report identifies risks: 'If capital or revenue costs rise faster than assumed, if inflation is above the modelled rate, if the children transferred in would otherwise have attracted lower external costs than the current modelling, or if voids exceed the modelled 10% allowance, the reserve will deplete more quickly and the point at which further corporate support is required will move forward.'
findings.matters: Sinking fund model is highly sensitive to cost and utilization variables; deterioration in any assumption could trigger need for corporate support sooner than Year 11, creating additional budget pressure.
findings.figures: Modeled inflation: 3% per annum; Modeled void rate: 10%; Modeled occupancy: 90%; Modeled external placement cost: £2.4m per annum
findings.quote: If capital or revenue costs rise faster than assumed, if inflation is above the modelled rate, if the children transferred in would otherwise have attracted lower external costs than the current modelling, or if voids exceed the modelled 10% allowance, the reserve will deplete more quickly and the point at which further corporate support is required will move forward

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Project timeline creates limited contingency between planned opening (April 2028) and Department for Education deadline (March 2029).
findings.detail: Council targets Ofsted registration by January 2028 and home opening by April 2028, with DfE funding deadline of March 2029. Report states: 'This leaves limited contingency, so the project will need to move at pace through planning, procurement, refurbishment, registration and mobilisation. Progress will be monitored through programme governance, with any slippage escalated quickly where it could affect the planned opening date.'
findings.matters: Limited contingency in complex multi-stage capital project with external regulatory gatekeeper creates delivery risk; slippage in planning, procurement or Ofsted registration could jeopardize DfE grant or require corporate support for extended holding costs.
findings.figures: DfE deadline: March 2029; Planned opening: April 2028; Ofsted registration target: January 2028; 11-month contingency window
findings.quote: This leaves limited contingency, so the project will need to move at pace through planning, procurement, refurbishment, registration and mobilisation

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Council reverses September 2024 Mayor and Cabinet decision approving three children's homes; now proposes single larger home instead.
findings.detail: In September 2024 Mayor and Cabinet approved three small children's homes in former school caretaker properties. Further feasibility work identified 'significant weaknesses in the previously approved approach' including 'duplicated staffing overheads, weaker operational resilience, viability concerns, safeguarding and registration risks.' Council now recommends single home at 200 Kirkdale. Report states it 'supersedes the decision of Mayor and Cabinet taken on 18th September 2024 insofar as it relates to the previously approved three-home delivery model.'
findings.matters: Substantial reversal of major capital project approved 22 months earlier indicates prior assessment was flawed or significant risk factors emerged post-approval; material changes to approved scope affect project credibility and delivery forecast.
findings.figures: Original decision: September 2024 three-home model; Revised decision: September 2026 single-home model
findings.quote: This report supersedes the decision of Mayor and Cabinet taken on 18th September 2024 insofar as it relates to the previously approved three-home delivery model

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Financial model indicates further corporate financial support will be required from Year 11 onwards, beyond current modeling period.
findings.detail: The 10-year financial model establishes a sinking fund for capital and lifecycle costs. However the council explicitly states the proposal 'does not remove the need for further corporate financial support in year 11 on the current assumptions.' The report notes that once operational the council will develop a longer-term lifecycle model to budget for costs beyond Year 10.
findings.matters: Proposal creates unquantified long-term financial commitment for the council in future budget cycles; currently unfunded costs will emerge within foreseeable timeframe.
findings.figures: 10-year model period; Year 11+ funding requirement identified but not quantified
findings.quote: does not remove the need for further corporate financial support in year 11 on the current assumptions

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Financial model depends on placement cost savings but the budget generating those savings is already overspending.
findings.detail: Model assumes £2.4m annual external placement costs versus £1.915m operating costs. Report explicitly states: 'FHC placement budgets are already overspending and therefore... the delivery of the home as modelled does not create net cost savings.' The council must recover an existing overspend in order for the assumed cost avoidance to fund the capital repayment and lifecycle costs.
findings.matters: Capital repayment depends on achieving savings in a budget already in deficit; this creates compounded budget pressure where the council must fix one problem to fund another.
findings.figures: £2.4m annual external placement costs assumed; £1.915m annual Kirkdale running costs; Family Help and Care placement budget currently overspending
findings.quote: FHC placement budgets are already overspending and therefore, while we should be able to fund the capital and lifecycle costs the delivery of the home as modelled does not create net cost savings

findings.paper_title: Capital investment to refurbish and operate a 5–6 bed local authority children’s home at 200 Kirkdale, Sydenham - Report
findings.headline: Council requires additional £479,000 capital funding beyond previously approved budget to complete Kirkdale refurbishment.
findings.detail: Total capital requirement is £1.68m, comprising £800,000 DfE grant, £400,000 capital receipt and £479,000 additional council capital funding. The additional amount is expected to be repaid through placement cost savings achieved in early years of operation. This represents unbudgeted capital addition to a major project.
findings.matters: Unplanned capital additions indicate project estimation accuracy and control; lenders track supplementary funding requests and their justification.
findings.figures: £479,000 additional capital requirement; £1.68m total; £800,000 DfE grant; £400,000 capital receipt
findings.quote: Note the additional £479,000 capital investment, bringing the total capital requirement to £1.68m as approved in the budget report that went to full council in July 2026

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: WorkWell funding is drawn down quarterly in arrears through quarterly invoicing to ICB
findings.detail: Lewisham will invoice the ICB on a quarterly basis to draw down funding. The ICB submits quarterly claims to DWP 'in arrears.' DWP then verifies and pays the ICB 'on a quarterly basis, in arrears.' This creates a cash flow lag: Lewisham must fund staff payroll and service delivery costs before receiving corresponding income from the ICB.
findings.matters: A finance director must ensure sufficient working capital or reserve capacity to cover quarterly staffing and delivery costs before receiving arrears payments from DWP via the ICB. This is particularly material given the rising participant targets in years 2-3.
findings.figures: Quarterly invoicing and quarterly arrears payment from DWP
findings.quote: The London Borough of Lewisham will invoice the ICB on a quarterly basis to draw down their Work Well funding each quarter... The DWP will verify the claim form and will pay the ICB for the total amount claimed, on a quarterly basis, in arrears.

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: SEL ICB must achieve at least 55% of its 890-participant Year 1 target (490 participants) or DWP will take performance management action
findings.detail: The DWP requires the South East London ICB to achieve at least 55% of agreed annual activity targets. If this is not met, 'the DWP will take performance management action.' Lewisham's 171-participant Year 1 target contributes to the collective SEL total, and 'the activity across all six SEL boroughs will be added together to reach this total.' Performance is assessed at ICB level, not by individual borough.
findings.matters: Lewisham's ability to secure continued funding and avoid DWP intervention depends partly on the collective performance of five other councils. If SEL underperforms, it could trigger funding restrictions or conditions affecting Lewisham despite Lewisham's own delivery performance.
findings.figures: 890 total participants required across SEL in Year 1; 55% threshold = 490 participants minimum
findings.quote: DWP require ICB's to achieve at least 55% of their agreed activity target each year, if this is not achieved the DWP will take performance management action.

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: Lewisham's WorkWell participation targets grow from 171 participants in Year 1 to 611 in Year 2 and 649 in Year 3
findings.detail: The council must recruit and employ Work and Health Coaches and Multi-Disciplinary Teams to deliver these participants. The Year 2 target is 3.6 times the Year 1 baseline and Year 3 is 3.8 times Year 1. The agreement makes the council 'responsible for the recruitment and employment of staff' to achieve these targets, creating significant staffing cost and recruitment commitments.
findings.matters: The steep growth in participation targets implies substantial payroll and recruitment costs ramping in years 2-3 to deliver a service that is itself conditionally funded. A finance director must plan for staffing and related delivery costs that may exceed available income if DWP does not confirm year 2-3 funding.
findings.figures: Year 1: 171 participants; Year 2: 611 participants; Year 3: 649 participants
findings.quote: WorkWell services are responsible for the recruitment and employment of staff. This must include Work and Health Coaches and Multi-Disciplinary Teams who deliver services

findings.paper_title: WorkWell – Expanding the health and employment integrated system in Lewisham - Appendix B - WorkWell Section 256-Lewisham and SELICB- V2
findings.headline: WorkWell funding for 2027/28 and 2028/29 is indicative and subject to DWP confirmation
findings.detail: Lewisham's Year 1 funding of £193,173 is confirmed, but Years 2 and 3 are explicitly conditional. The agreement states: 'The funding allocations for 2027/28 and 2028/29 are indicative figures and are subject to confirmation of funding from the DWP.' This creates budget planning risk as half the three-year income stream cannot be guaranteed.
findings.matters: A finance director must plan for the possibility that confirmed budget income for years 2-3 does not materialise, forcing reprioritisation of spending or staffing reductions mid-programme.
findings.quote: a further £499,672 in 2027/28 and £541,423 in 2028/29 subject to further confirmation of WorkWell funding allocation to SEL ICB by the Department of Work and Pensions (DWP)

findings.paper_title: Contract Award Report for Electric Vehicle Charging Point Installation, Operation and Maintenance - Part 1
findings.headline: Both contractors pass financial viability assessment with credit scores exceeding council minimum thresholds
findings.detail: Believ Limited credit score 72 (very low risk, significantly exceeds council minimum of 30); Zest Eco Limited credit score 70 (low risk, exceeds minimum threshold). Zest Eco reported a loss for year ending December 2024 but maintains strong balance sheet with high proportion of assets funded through equity and significant fixed assets. Both contractors required to provide Parent Company Guarantees or Performance Bonds prior to signing.
findings.matters: Mitigates supplier default risk over contract period; financial failure of either contractor could disrupt EV infrastructure delivery and revenue to council.
findings.figures: Believ Limited Creditsafe score: 72 (minimum acceptable: 30); Zest Eco Limited Creditsafe score: 70
findings.quote: A Creditsafe financial assessment of Believ Ltd indicates a credit score of 72, representing a very low risk and significantly exceeding the Council's minimum acceptable score of 30

findings.paper_title: Contract Award Report for Electric Vehicle Charging Point Installation, Operation and Maintenance - Part 1
findings.headline: £2.981m grant funding from Office for Zero Emission Vehicles and £183,000 from Department for Transport de-risks concession structure
findings.detail: The council secured £2.981m in grant funding from OZEV (split equally with Greenwich and held separately by each authority) under the Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure scheme, with maximum public sector contribution of £993,666.66 per lot across both boroughs. Additional £183,000 DfT grant for cross-pavement charging trial (capital only, with non-capital costs to be met from service budgets).
findings.matters: Central government grant support reduces private investment burden and improves financial viability of the concession model, reducing market risk and revenue assumptions.
findings.figures: £2,981,000 (OZEV, split with Greenwich); £993,666.66 per lot maximum grant contribution; £183,000 (DfT)
findings.quote: The Council has secured £2.981m in grant funding in partnership with Greenwich Council from the Office for Zero Emission Vehicles (OZEV) under the Local Electric Vehicle Infrastructure (LEVI) Scheme

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report
findings.headline: TfL has reserved right to provide additional LIP funding mid-year, creating mid-year funding uncertainty
findings.detail: The TfL grant letter confirms an initial allocation of £2,557,000 but explicitly reserves the right to make further funding available later in 2026/27 'subject to progress.' This creates uncertainty over the full-year budget available and makes end-of-year position dependent on mid-year progress review.
findings.matters: Programme funding is not finalized for the full year; a council or lender needs to understand that some capital programmes are contingent on satisfactory progress reporting and could face mid-year increases or reductions.
findings.figures: Initial TfL allocation £2,557,000; further funding available 'later within 2026/27 subject to progress'
findings.quote: An initial allocation of £2,557,000 was confirmed in the grant letter from TfL. The letter highlighted that further funding can be made available later within 2026/27 subject to progress.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report
findings.headline: TfL Local Implementation Plan funding of £2.56m carries clawback provision if grant conditions are breached
findings.detail: Section 10.1 states that LIP funding has conditions attached, and if breached 'the Council could potentially be required to pay some or all these funds back to the DfT.' Annual grant returns are required to demonstrate compliance, creating ongoing compliance risk.
findings.matters: The LIP funding represents 40% of the total capital programme (£2.56m of £6.3m from all sources). Clawback would be material; the council needs to maintain internal controls to avoid breach and loss of funding.
findings.figures: TfL LIP allocation £2,557,000; of which £2,325,000 is capital
findings.quote: The Local Implementation Plan (LIP) funding has conditions attached that the Council must adhere to. If these conditions are breached, then the Council could potentially be required to pay some or all these funds back to the DfT.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report
findings.headline: DfT Local Highway Maintenance funding of £633,000 is performance-based incentive component alongside £1,004,000 baseline
findings.detail: Of the £1,637,000 received from DfT, only £1,004,000 is baseline funding. The remaining £633,000 is conditional incentive funding, meaning it is not guaranteed if the council does not meet the performance conditions the DfT attaches to it.
findings.matters: Loss of the incentive element would reduce the highways budget by 17% (£633k of £3.8m), forcing either further reserve draw or programme reduction. The council's ability to retain this funding depends on meeting DfT performance requirements.
findings.figures: Incentive funding £633,000; baseline funding £1,004,000; total DfT allocation £1,637,000
findings.quote: £1,637,000 of this is funded through DfT's Local Highway Maintenance Capital Funding 2026-2030, consisting of £1,004,000 baseline and £633,000 incentive funding

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report
findings.headline: Budget carries explicit risk of overrun requiring additional approval, with further funding likely from reserves or external borrowing
findings.detail: Section 10.3 identifies that the approved budget may be exceeded due to unforeseen costs. Any overrun would require additional approval from Mayor and Cabinet, and the council flags that additional funding would 'likely be a call on the Council's reserves or external borrowing, unless additional funding was sourced.'
findings.matters: Material budget risk flagged by the council itself; overrun could trigger either reserve draw-down or new borrowing, both of which affect the council's financial position and debt levels.
findings.figures: Approved budget £3,809,259.03
findings.quote: As outlined in section 12, there is a risk that the approved budget might be exceeded due to unforeseen costs. These additional costs would require additional budget and further funding, which will need to be approved by Mayor and Cabinet. This additional funding would likely be a call on the Council's reserves or external borrowing, unless additional funding was sourced.

findings.paper_title: 2026-27 Strategic Transport and Highways Capital Programme - Report
findings.headline: Approximately 56% of the £3.8m highways capital budget is funded from council capital reserves
findings.detail: The £3,809,259.03 Highways and Bridges budget comprises £1,637,000 from DfT Local Highway Maintenance funding, £27,000 from TfL Principal Road Renewal, leaving approximately £2.1m to be funded from the council's own capital reserves. This represents material commitment of the council's capital resources to highways maintenance.
findings.matters: Finance directors and lenders need to understand the proportion of capital spending coming from the council's own reserves versus external sources, and whether this rate is sustainable given competing capital priorities and reserve depletion.
findings.figures: Total budget £3,809,259.03; DfT funding £1,637,000; TfL funding £27,000; reserves funding approximately £2,145,259
findings.quote: £1,637,000 of this is funded through DfT's Local Highway Maintenance Capital Funding 2026-2030, consisting of £1,004,000 baseline and £633,000 incentive funding, and £27,000 through TfL's Principal Road Renewal programme. The remaining amount is funded through the Council's Capital Reserves.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Council maintains under-borrowed position of £329m internal borrowing in 2026/27 based on interest rate assumptions
findings.detail: Council continues deliberate strategy of funding capital through cash reserves (internal borrowing) rather than external debt, with forecast internal borrowing of £329m in 2026/27. Strategy is based on assumption that investment returns remain lower than borrowing costs, but this depends on interest rate path.
findings.matters: Shows confidence in interest rate forecasts and ability to manage liquidity; signals vulnerability to rate shock—if borrowing costs fall faster than expected, internal borrowing becomes more expensive than external debt and strategy would reverse.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £329m (2026/27); CFR £731.9m less external borrowing £234.9m = £497m of internal borrowing need met from reserves
findings.quote: The Council is currently maintaining an under-borrowed position. This means that the capital borrowing need, (the Capital Financing Requirement), has not been fully funded with loan debt as cash supporting the Council's reserves, balances and cash flow has been used as an alternative funding measure.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Financing costs ratio rises to 18.0% of net revenue stream for 2026/27 (from 15.9% actual 2025/26)
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream is forecast to rise to 18.0% in 2026/27 from 15.9% in 2025/26, reflecting impact of expanded capital programme and increased external borrowing. Excluding PFI, the ratio rises from 4.8% to 6.0%, showing underlying growth in debt service burden.
findings.matters: Growing ratio of debt service to revenue indicates rising revenue pressure from capital programme; signals approach to unsustainability if ratio continues to climb beyond 2026/27.
findings.figures: 2026/27 estimate 18.0% vs 2025/26 actual 15.9%; excluding PFI: 6.0% vs 4.8%
findings.quote: 2025/26 Actual 2026/27 Estimate 2027/28 Estimate 2028/29 Estimate: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 15.9% 18.0% 16.2% 15.5%

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Investment portfolio yield declines to 3.7% from 4.6% year-on-year as rates expected to fall
findings.detail: The Council's £210m investment portfolio (30 June 2026) yields 3.7% compared to 4.6% one year earlier. Council expects further yield compression as it depletes cash reserves to fund capital programme and as Bank of England base rates fall from 3.75% forecast through mid-2027.
findings.matters: Declining investment income reduces revenue resources available for services and affects treasury net cost position; signals tightening of cash position as capital programme consumes reserves.
findings.figures: 3.7% yield on £210m investments (30 June 2026) vs 4.6% at June 2025; investments down from £264m (2025) to £210m
findings.quote: The Council held £210m of investments as at 30 June 2026 (£185.1m at 31 March 2026) and the current annualised yield as at 30 June 2026 is 3.7% (compared to 4.6% at June 2025).

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Prudential borrowing of £72.6m planned for 2026/27 (£42.0m General Fund, £30.6m HRA)
findings.detail: Council intends to take on £72.6m of new external borrowing in 2026/27 to fund expanded capital programme. Over the full four-year forecast (2026–30), total prudential borrowing is £51.6m (General Fund) and £198.2m (HRA), showing material increase in external debt.
findings.matters: Signals substantial new debt issuance; lenders need to understand scale of borrowing requirement against capital programme expansion and existing CFR of £731.9m.
findings.quote: The table below shows the required prudential borrowing required in 2026/27 which is £42.0m for the general fund and £30.6m for the HRA.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Council repays £17.5m of LOBO loans in first five months of 2026/27 as part of two-year reduction strategy
findings.detail: Lewisham has systematically reduced LOBO exposure from £119.7m (at end 2023/24) to £54.3m (31 March 2026), and repaid a further £17.5m in the first five months of 2026/27. This reflects active response to rising rates through exercise of borrower redemption options when lenders call.
findings.matters: LOBO repayments are significant liquidity events; demonstrates council's risk management in rising rate environment and reduces exposure to future rate reset risk.
findings.figures: LOBO loans reduced £119.7m to £54.3m over two years; £17.5m repaid 1 April–30 June 2026
findings.quote: In the last two years the Council has reduced its LOBO loans from £119.7m to £54.3m as at 31 March 2026. Since 1 April 2026 the Council has repaid a further £17.5m of LOBO loans.

findings.paper_title: Treasury Management Outturn and Mid-Year Review 2026-27 - Report
findings.headline: Capital Programme for 2026-30 increases to £684.6m from £421.4m approved in March 2026
findings.detail: The capital programme expanded by £263.2m (62%) in three months, driven primarily by HRA housing investment of £219.7m. This materially changes the Council's funding requirement and borrowing need for the period.
findings.matters: A major unplanned increase in capital spend drives material change in borrowing requirements, revenue financing costs, and liquidity planning; critical context for lenders assessing debt trajectory.
findings.figures: £684.6m forecast 2026-30 vs £421.4m approved March 2026; increase of £263.2m
findings.quote: The Capital Programme for 2026-30 was agreed as £421.4m in March 2026 and is now forecast to be £684.6m as at 30 June 2026, an increase of £263.2m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Building for Lewisham Strategic Partner scheme commits £95.8m while completing procurement
findings.detail: The council has included £95.8m for the first schemes (Thomas Lane Yard and Achilles regeneration phases 1-2) dependent on completing a Strategic Partner procurement. This major scheme experienced £11.4m slippage in the previous year.
findings.matters: This represents 12% of the full capital programme committed dependent on completing a procurement. Given the historical slippage on this programme, delivery and funding risk are material for lenders.
findings.figures: £95.8m budget for first schemes; prior year BfL slippage £11.4m (55% of budget)
findings.quote: A key delivery mechanism is the conclusion of the procurement of a Strategic Partner. This has resulted in the inclusion of the programme and the £95.8m budget needed for the first schemes.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Contingent £775.73m GLA housing grant bid, with £50.99m additional borrowing if approved
findings.detail: The council has bid for £775.73m of affordable housing grant from the GLA to deliver 3,070 homes over 10 years. If successful, this would increase the capital programme by £169.5m over four years and trigger £50.99m additional borrowing. The bid outcome is not yet known and any approval will require Mayor and Cabinet decision.
findings.matters: This massive contingent commitment creates material forecast uncertainty. If the bid succeeds, borrowing increases significantly; if it fails, housing delivery targets may be missed. Lenders need clarity on which scenario is planned for.
findings.figures: £775.73m grant bid pending; potential programme increase £169,516,311 over four years; potential additional borrowing £50,991,293
findings.quote: The Council has put forward an ambitious bid to the GLA for £775.73m of affordable housing grant to deliver 3,070 homes over for the next 10 years. Whilst we are yet to hear the outcome from this... if successful this could increase the programme over the next four years by £169,516,311

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: £10m contingency funded from reserves for urgent risks and pressures
findings.detail: The council has included a £10m contingency budget (split between HRA and general fund) funded from reserves to cover urgent works that preclude formal member approval in advance. Use of this contingency will draw down reserves and be reported to members retrospectively.
findings.matters: Reserve-funded contingencies indicate either incomplete budgeting for known risks or identified-but-unquantified pressures. Drawing reserves to fund contingencies indicates pressure on the council's financial cushion.
findings.figures: £10m contingency budget across HRA and general fund, funded from reserves
findings.quote: The inclusion of a £10m contingency budget into the 2026/27 budget... will ensure that works of an urgent nature can be delivered. The £10m, if needed, will be funded from reserves in 2026/27

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: £293.2m of external borrowing committed across the expanded capital programme
findings.detail: The council is committing £293.2m of prudential borrowing to deliver the current capital programme: £51.5m from the general fund and £241.7m from the HRA. The council states this remains within Treasury Management Strategy tolerances, but represents material debt commitment.
findings.matters: High borrowing levels constrain future financial flexibility and increase debt servicing costs. Lenders need to assess whether debt levels are sustainable and whether there is headroom for additional borrowing if external funding sources fail.
findings.figures: £293.2m total external borrowing (£51.5m general fund; £241.7m HRA)
findings.quote: The agreed budget forecast £293.2m of external borrowing to deliver the current programme, meaning that the decisions within this report would not breach the agreed Treasury Management Strategy (TMS)

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Capital programme increased by £231.1m (43%) in a single update cycle
findings.detail: The approved capital programme was expanded from £539.3m (March 2026 budget) to £770.3m, a net increase of £231.1m. This includes £95.8m for the Building for Lewisham Strategic Partner schemes and £68m added to future HRA years to align with the 30-year business plan.
findings.matters: A 43% programme expansion in a single update signals either incomplete original planning or significant replanning between March and July. For lenders, this raises questions about forecast accuracy and financial control.
findings.figures: £28.3m increase for 2026/27; £202.7m increase for 2027/28 onward; total net increase £231.1m
findings.quote: Agree that the cumulative impact of all the above recommendations is a net increase of £28.3m for 2026/27 and an increase of £202.7m for 2027/28 onward, totalling a net increase to the full Capital Programme of £231.1m.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme Budget
findings.headline: Significant capital programme slippage in 2025/26, particularly in major housing schemes
findings.detail: The council's capital programme outturn was £139.4m against a budget of £178.1m, a £38.7m (21.7%) underspend. The Building for Lewisham HRA programme specifically underperformed by £11.4m (budget £20.8m, outturn £9.4m). The main HRA capital programme (Decent Homes) also slipped by £18.8m.
findings.matters: Large slippage indicates delivery risk on the council's major housing and infrastructure schemes. For lenders, this means timelines for homes delivery, community benefits, infrastructure development, and debt servicing may slip.
findings.figures: £139.4m outturn against £178.1m budget (£38.7m slippage = 21.7%); Building for Lewisham HRA: £9.4m outturn against £20.8m budget (£11.4m shortfall)
findings.quote: This shows an outturn of £139.4m against a budget of £178.1m, indicating a slippage of £38.7m at year end.

findings.paper_title: Capital Programme July Council 2026
findings.headline: Council acknowledges risk that capital projects may overspend allocated budgets
findings.detail: The report states that despite project budgets including contingencies, there is a risk of project overspends. If overspends occur, the Council will seek additional budget to cover the shortfall.
findings.matters: Acknowledged risk suggests contingencies may prove insufficient, creating potential for additional funding demands beyond the approved programme.

findings.detail: The HRA 30-year business plan has been updated, adding £68m of capital spending for future years. Funding comprises £31m from Major Repairs Reserve, £6m revenue contribution, and £31m additional borrowing.
findings.matters: Significant additions to planned HRA investment suggest material changes in housing renewal requirements; the funding split indicates increased future debt service.

findings.detail: The updated capital programme is funded by £293.2m of prudential borrowing (£241.7m HRA, £51.5m GF). This represents a substantial increase requiring review as part of the Treasury Management Strategy update.
