findings.paper_title: Council - 26-11-25 - Appendix B - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_FINAL DRAFT_171125
findings.headline: Auditors flagged specific management override risk in HRA reserves due to three-year pattern of depletion and pressure
findings.detail: The auditors identified a specific fraud risk of management override in relation to HRA reserves, noting the reserves balance has fallen over three years and is under significant pressure. They flagged increased risk that management could inappropriately transfer HRA expenditure to the general fund, as the Authority is not permitted to be in HRA deficit.
findings.matters: Control weaknesses where financial pressure could incentivize inappropriate accounting transfers signal governance risk to lenders and finance directors
findings.figures: HRA reserves £18.6m at 31 March 2025, above 10% of rental and service charge income; prior year £7.4m was below target
findings.quote: We have identified a specific risk of management override of controls in relation to HRA reserves. The reserves balance has fallen over the past three years and is under significant pressure. As the Authority is not permitted to be in a HRA fund deficit there is an increased risk of management override which we anticipate could occur by transferring HRA expenditure to the general fund.

findings.paper_title: Council - 26-11-25 - Appendix C - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: Level 3 investment valuations used mid-prices instead of required bid prices; £998k correction applied
findings.detail: Auditors found that LCIV fund valuations were overstated by £998k because management used mid prices instead of bid prices for year-end valuations. IFRS 13 requires the use of prices within the bid-ask spread most representative of fair value. The error was corrected but indicates gaps in the pension fund's investment valuation process.
findings.matters: Even though the adjustment is immaterial (0.05% of fund), it reveals the pension fund administrator could not obtain required bid price data and fell back to a non-compliant method, suggesting procedural gaps that could mask larger issues.
findings.figures: £998k overstatement; Level 3 pooled investments represent £513.61m or 27.29% of total fund assets (£1,882.32m)
findings.quote: This misstatement occurs as management use mid prices report instead of bid prices due to non availability of bid prices at the time of preparing the accounts.

findings.paper_title: Council - 26-11-25 - Appendix C - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: Active member reconciliation not completed; prior-year finding re-raised for second year
findings.detail: The audit recommendation from 2023/24 to perform annual member reconciliation was only partially implemented. Pensioner reconciliation was completed, but reconciliation of active members to payroll records remains undone. The council is now pushing this to September 2026.
findings.matters: Inability to verify active member records against payroll creates risk that pension entitlements are incorrectly recorded, which could emerge as material liabilities that the council must fund.
findings.figures: Active members: reconciliation outstanding; only pensioner reconciliation completed
findings.quote: This has been implemented as at 31 March 2025 in respect of the reconciliation for pensioners, however, the original recommendation included active members, which the council did not reconcile, and therefore we have re-raised this.

findings.paper_title: Council - 26-11-25 - Appendix C - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: Priority One control deficiency: departing staff system access not disabled promptly
findings.detail: Auditors identified one instance where a leaver's user account in the Oracle system was not disabled in a timely manner after departure. Management could not provide direct system evidence confirming no access occurred after termination, only an editable file. This control gap creates risk of unauthorized access or data misuse by former employees.
findings.matters: Control gaps in pension administration affect data security and indicate broader weaknesses in the council's control environment that could affect management of financial records.
findings.figures: One identified instance; system: Oracle
findings.quote: During our testing, we identified one instance where a leaver's user account within the Oracle system was not disabled in a timely manner after the employee's departure.

findings.paper_title: 7. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_2024_25 VfM_DRAFT
findings.headline: General government funding reform expected to increase financial pressure on London Boroughs, including Lewisham, through amended allocation formula
findings.detail: While government intends to increase overall local government funding in 2025-26, the amended funding formula is expected to hit London Boroughs particularly hard. Lewisham has considered the impact in its Medium Term Financial Strategy but will require formal updating once the formula is known, adding uncertainty to the £30m savings target.
findings.matters: Anticipated funding reductions narrow headroom already tight from savings underperformance; scale of impact unknown and could worsen the council's financial position
findings.figures: Impact of funding formula change not quantified in this paper
findings.quote: The Local Government Funding Reform is expected to increase the overall available funding to Local Government in 2025-26, however, the impact of negative changes in allocation through the amended funding formula is expected to increase financial pressure on London Boroughs and on the Authority which will have consequences for the scale of savings required.

findings.paper_title: 7. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_2024_25 VfM_DRAFT
findings.headline: 17% of council housing stock does not meet Decent Homes Standard as at 30 June 2025, down from 26% at March 2024, following December 2023 self-referral to regulator
findings.detail: The council self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing in December 2023 after identifying failures to meet statutory health and safety requirements, including fire remedial actions and repairs. A stock condition survey has since revealed 17% of homes do not meet the Decent Homes Standard as at 30 June 2025 (improved from 26% at March 2024). The Housing Ombudsman published a special investigation report with five themes including hazards, communication and contract management.
findings.matters: Regulatory action, sustained non-compliance, and ombudsman intervention create reputational and operational risk; remediation costs are uncertain and ongoing
findings.figures: 17% of stock not meeting Decent Homes Standard as at 30 June 2025 (down from 26%); over 1,600 category one hazards reduced in severity or closed
findings.quote: The Authority self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing in December 2023 due to identifying a failure to meet statutory health and safety requirements in some of its homes, including overdue fire remedial actions and repairs.

findings.paper_title: 7. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_2024_25 VfM_DRAFT
findings.headline: HRA remains in significant deficit (£46.2m) despite improvement, driven by inflation, rent reductions and housing compliance obligations
findings.detail: While the HRA deficit improved from £88.3m in 2023/24, the 2024/25 actual deficit of £46.2m against a planned £0m shows the service remains structurally challenged. Pressures include inflation on repairs costs, central government-imposed rent reductions, and obligations from the self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing regarding health and safety compliance.
findings.matters: HRA deficits directly deplete council reserves and signal unsustainable service economics; regulatory pressures compound the financial risk
findings.figures: Actual HRA deficit (£46.2m) in 2024/25 vs planned £0m; prior year (£88.3m); reserves topped up to £18.6m
findings.quote: The Authority also has well-documented financial pressures in relation to the HRA caused by the impact of inflation, costs for housing works and materials, real-terms rent reductions imposed by Central Government, obligations to improve the safety of homes and additional pressure as a result of the self-referral to the Regulator of Social Housing in 2023/24.

findings.paper_title: 7. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_2024_25 VfM_DRAFT
findings.headline: Prior-year savings targets continue to underperform, new £30m savings required across 2025-26 and 2026-27
findings.detail: The council set £8.0m in agreed savings for 2024/25 plus undelivered prior-year targets, but throughout the year services that overspent previously continued to face pressures above budget. The 2025-26 budget now carries a £30m savings target over two years with £29.25m already identified, implying significant delivery risk.
findings.matters: Persistent savings underperformance signals budget control weakness; the scale of new targets (£30m over two years) creates material delivery risk that could lead to further reserve drawdowns
findings.figures: £8.0m agreed savings target for 2024/25; £30m savings target for next two years with £29.25m identified
findings.quote: We note that underperformance in savings in 2024/25 is well reported and understood, for example, savings and overspend reduction measures for the 2024/25 and 2025/26 budget gap were reported to Mayor and Cabinet on 4 December 2024.

findings.paper_title: 7. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_2024_25 VfM_DRAFT
findings.headline: Children and Young People services overspent by £15.3m in 2024/25 despite prior-year focus
findings.detail: The council reported a £15.3m overspend in Children and Young People services in 2024/25 (down from £18.3m at Period 10). The council performed a deep dive on this service in 2023/24, invested in cost tracking and established a Governance Group Board, yet spending pressures persisted above budgeted levels.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether cost control measures in this volatile, demand-driven service are effective or whether further overspends are likely
findings.figures: £15.3m overspend in Children and Young People in 2024/25; £18.3m at Period 10
findings.quote: The Authority are reporting a £19m overspend across all services in 2024/25, £15.3m of which is for Children and Young People, though this was reduced from £18.3m reported at Period 10.

findings.paper_title: 2a. Minutes 2025 07 22 DRAFT - Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: PSTN telephone network switch-off delayed to January 2027, creating extended cost exposure if December 2025 project deadline is missed
findings.detail: A new corporate risk was added for the PSTN switch-off, initially planned for December 2025. Government has confirmed there will not be a hard switch-off, allowing telephone lines to continue functioning until January 2027 at increased cost. The final cost is still uncertain, with concern that any failure to meet the December 2025 internal project deadline will result in further cost escalation.
findings.matters: Unbudgeted infrastructure costs from utility provider mandates add unexpected pressure to a council already managing budget deficits and reserve drawdowns.
findings.figures: Cost increase for lines continuing to January 2027; amount uncertain; December 2025 internal deadline at risk
findings.quote: There is concern that those unable to meet the December 2025 deadline may experience increased costs for any extensions beyond that date, though this remains speculative.

findings.paper_title: 2a. Minutes 2025 07 22 DRAFT - Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Internal audit capacity constraints reduced coverage in adult social care and health, with six high-risk audit recommendations outstanding for over 18 months
findings.detail: The Head of Assurance reported that internal audits completed this year have decreased, with particular audit coverage gaps in adult social care and health due to deferrals and incomplete work. Of 13 overdue audit actions, six recommendations have remained open for over 18 months. The overall audit action completion rate reached 77%, but priority focus is needed on resolving high-risk recommendations promptly rather than tracking numbers alone.
findings.matters: Reduced audit coverage in material service areas plus extended delays in addressing high-risk findings represents a governance weakness that increases the risk of undetected problems in the council's largest budget headings.
findings.figures: 77% action completion rate; 13 overdue issues; 6 outstanding over 18 months; audit coverage reduced from prior years
findings.quote: Concerns were raised regarding reduced audit coverage, particularly within directorates such as adult social care and health; deferrals or incomplete internal audits contributed to this lighter coverage across key areas.

findings.paper_title: 2a. Minutes 2025 07 22 DRAFT - Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Financial sustainability risk score lowered despite ongoing reliance on reserves to balance budget and delayed Medium-Term Financial Strategy review
findings.detail: The committee questioned whether the reduction in the financial sustainability risk score (LBL 010) was justified, noting the balanced budget still relies on reserves and funding uncertainty remains high. The MTFS review is delayed, required savings have not yet been delivered, and government consultations have given only partial clarity. Officers acknowledged the risk score is expected to rise in September when more information becomes available, and anticipated that expected reductions in financial settlement over the next three years will push the risk rating higher.
findings.matters: Lowering the financial sustainability risk while the underlying drivers of pressure remain unresolved suggests either over-optimism or a need for more transparent assessment; a council dependent on reserve drawdowns faces mounting stress if savings targets slip.
findings.figures: Three-year reduction in financial settlement expected
findings.quote: the risk level will rise, especially given the expected reduction in financial settlement over the next three years. The risk register is likely to show a higher risk rating in September as more information becomes available.

findings.paper_title: 2a. Minutes 2025 07 22 DRAFT - Audit and Risk Committee
findings.headline: Local special educational needs deficit of £18 million would require council reserves to cover if statutory override is withdrawn
findings.detail: The committee heard that Lewisham's SEND deficit stands at £18 million. Under current law this would need to be funded from council reserves without the statutory override that allows schools to run deficits. The override has been extended for two years with a government consultation expected in autumn on possible accounting and policy changes; nationally the SEND deficit is approximately £1.5 billion.
findings.matters: A material SEND deficit contingent on statutory overrides represents a significant future liability that depends on government policy decisions beyond the council's control, and will force reserve drawdown if the override is withdrawn.
findings.figures: £18 million local SEND deficit; £1.5 billion national; override extended two years
findings.quote: The local special educational needs deficit now stands at £18 million. Without the override, the local authority would need to cover this from reserves.

findings.paper_title: 5. Internal Audit Progress Report November 2025
findings.headline: Council's internal audit function is not compliant with Global Internal Audit Standards and lacks required audit strategy
findings.detail: Self-assessment against Global Internal Audit Standards identified compliance gaps. The most significant is that the council has not yet developed and approved an Internal Audit Strategy as required by the standards. A full list of required improvements will be presented to a future committee.
findings.matters: Professional audit standards compliance reflects governance maturity; a council out of compliance may have governance gaps affecting how effectively it identifies and responds to financial and operational risks.
findings.figures: Global Internal Audit Standards self-assessment completed; Internal Audit Strategy not yet developed
findings.quote: Most significantly there is a requirement for an Internal Audit Strategy to be developed and approved by senior management and the Audit and Risk Committee.

findings.paper_title: 5. Internal Audit Progress Report November 2025
findings.headline: 20% of audit recommendations across the council remain overdue, including 2 high-priority housing actions from 4+ years ago
findings.detail: Of 73 open management actions, 15 are overdue. Housing has 8 overdue actions including 2 high priority; Corporate Services has 4 overdue actions from an IT Asset Management audit in 2023. While improved quarterly tracking processes have been introduced, the council is still working through a backlog of unimplemented recommendations.
findings.matters: Implementing audit recommendations is fundamental to building an effective control environment; overdue actions indicate the council takes time to close identified gaps, which could delay resolution of control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 20% of 73 actions overdue (~15 actions); Housing 8 overdue (2 high priority); Corporate Services 4 overdue from 2023 IT audit
findings.quote: Of the 73 management actions currently open, 80% are not yet due, with the remaining 20% overdue for implementation.

findings.paper_title: 5. Internal Audit Progress Report November 2025
findings.headline: Housing controls identified as requiring 18 recommendations across data quality, financial controls and oversight
findings.detail: The responsive repairs/DLO consultancy audit resulted in 18 agreed recommendations focused on data quality, financial controls and quality assurance. Additionally, the Selective Licensing Scheme audit identified 7 medium-severity findings including incorrect licence issue dates, missing documentation, and ineffective inspection processes. Multiple further housing audits are planned across safety compliance, tenancy management and repairs.
findings.matters: Housing represents a major council capital and revenue budget; control weaknesses in data quality and financial controls directly affect the reliability of financial reporting and service delivery.
findings.figures: 18 recommendations agreed for responsive repairs/DLO; 7 medium findings in Selective Licensing Scheme audit
findings.quote: Internal Audit worked with the service to agreed 18 recommendations to develop and improve controls. The themes of these recommendations related to data quality, financial controls and quality assurance and oversight.

findings.paper_title: 4c. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix C
findings.headline: Prior period adjustment: the Authority erroneously recorded £40.5m of internal borrowing as revenue contributions to capital in 2020/21 and 2021/22.
findings.detail: In 2019, the Authority approved a Housing Revenue Account new build programme to be financed by external borrowing. In 2020/21 and 2021/22, due to reserve levels and borrowing costs at the time, it used internal borrowing instead, but erroneously accounted for £13.9m and £26.6m respectively as revenue contributions to capital, incorrectly reducing the HRA Capital Financing Requirement. A prior period adjustment is now being made to reverse these entries and correctly recognise them as borrowing.
findings.matters: A £40.5m accounting error undetected in prior years indicates a significant weakness in the Authority's accounting controls and review processes. Lenders assess financial management quality through the strength of internal controls; errors of this magnitude raise questions about the reliability of the Authority's financial reporting and governance.
findings.quote: In 2020/21 and 2021/22 the Authority erroneously accounted for these as revenue contributions to capital outlay of £13.9m and £26.6m respectively and reduced the HRA Capital Financing Requirement in each year by these amounts.

findings.paper_title: 4a. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Significant Council Tax and NNDR credit balances outstanding for several years requiring write-off or refund
findings.detail: Council holds 'significant credit balances on Council Tax and NNDR accounts due to residents and businesses. These balances have remained outstanding for several years.' The council is taking action to refund these sums or write them off where customers cannot be traced and legal time limits have expired.
findings.matters: Aged creditor balances represent cash management inefficiency and collection control weaknesses. Large unresolved balances tie up cash and suggest billing/collection processes need improvement.
findings.figures: Not quantified; described as 'significant'; write-offs to be reported to Director of Finance
findings.quote: The Council has significant credit balances on Council Tax and NNDR accounts due to residents and businesses. These balances have remained outstanding for several years.

findings.paper_title: 4a. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: PFI contracts expiring in next 18 months; enhanced monitoring underway but documentation gaps previously identified
findings.detail: Auditors identified 'lack of record keeping of monitoring of PFI arrangements and difficulty by the Authority obtaining detailed information from PFI contractors about work completed, in respect of lifecycle replacement costs.' As of 11 November 2025, council notes 'enhanced monitoring of the housing PFI as part of the preparation and engagement for the expiry of this contract' and 'The Authority is introducing a review into PFI contracts which are expiring in the next 18 months.'
findings.matters: PFI contract expiries represent material financial events. Lenders need confidence that the council understands and can account for the costs and obligations involved. Documentation gaps create audit risk and operational uncertainty.
findings.figures: Multiple arrangements: streetlighting, Brockley, housing; housing PFI expiring within 18 months of 11 November 2025
findings.quote: lack of record keeping of monitoring of PFI arrangements and difficulty by the Authority obtaining detailed information from PFI contractors about work completed, in respect of lifecycle replacement costs

findings.paper_title: 4a. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: IFRS 16 quantitative impact assessment delayed, creating risk of material financial statement errors
findings.detail: Auditors noted that although Lewisham included only qualitative disclosures in 2023/24, 'it is expected that management should be well advanced in their quantitative impact assessment for the 2024-25 financial statements.' They warned 'There is a risk that delaying this assessment could lead to errors, insufficient review time, and potentially material misstatements.' Standard effective date was 1 April 2024.
findings.matters: IFRS 16 is a major accounting change affecting how leases appear on the balance sheet. Material errors in implementation could affect covenant calculations and lenders' understanding of the council's true financial position.
findings.figures: IFRS 16 effective 1 April 2024; due date for completion April 2025, with extension to 30 June 2025 for draft accounts
findings.quote: There is a risk that delaying this assessment could lead to errors, insufficient review time, and potentially material misstatements.

findings.paper_title: 4a. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix A
findings.headline: Nine of 15 tested lease agreements could not be located, creating IFRS 16 compliance risk
findings.detail: External auditors identified that 60% of sampled lease agreements are missing or not properly retained. This creates a material risk for IFRS 16 implementation in 2024/25 accounts. As of 11 November 2025, the status remains 'On Going' with the note that 'More work is still needed in this area.' The council acknowledges this will delay preparation of lease-related disclosures.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that lease obligations are properly documented and accounted for. Incomplete lease records directly affect the accuracy of the financial statements and could indicate broader documentation control weaknesses.
findings.figures: 9 of 15 leases tested could not be located; due date for comprehensive review extended to December 2025
findings.quote: In a sample of 15 lease agreements selected for testing, nine of the agreements could not be located. [...] More work is still needed in this area.

findings.paper_title: 4b. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix B
findings.headline: Audit found one instance where an employee's system access in Oracle was not disabled in a timely manner after departure.
findings.detail: Testing identified that a leaver's Oracle account was not promptly disabled after termination, and the council could not independently verify no unauthorized access occurred post-departure. The council will implement automated account disablement on termination date, use system-generated audit evidence, distribute daily leavers reports to IT, and conduct quarterly monitoring by Information Governance.
findings.matters: Failure to promptly revoke system access increases risk of unauthorized data access, data leakage, or misuse of organizational resources, weakening the control environment.
findings.figures: One instance identified; implementation deadline April 2026; quarterly monitoring to be introduced
findings.quote: During our testing, we identified one instance where a leaver's user account within the Oracle system was not disabled in a timely manner after the employee's departure.

findings.paper_title: 4b. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update - Appendix B
findings.headline: Housing Ombudsman special investigation identified systemic failures across five areas of housing service delivery.
findings.detail: The Ombudsman investigated cases from July-October 2024 and found failures in hazards, communication with residents, contract management, information management and systems. The council has initiated a Housing Improvement Plan to address these issues, including a new repairs system (November 2025), increased in-house repairs, and improved contractor management and staff training. This plan will be monitored monthly with the Regulator of Social Housing.
findings.matters: The council is under regulatory scrutiny from the Regulator of Social Housing and has identified systemic service failures requiring sustained improvement, which could affect operational capacity and borrowing perception.
findings.figures: Five emerging themes identified; investigation period July-October 2024; new repairs system November 2025; monthly monitoring meetings with regulator
findings.quote: The Housing Ombudsman published a special investigation report into the Authority. This report considered cases which were determined between July and October 2024 and had five emerging themes including hazards, communication with residents, contract management, knowledge and information management and systems.

findings.paper_title: 4. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - External Audit Update
findings.headline: Pension fund payroll reconciliation between Altair and Oracle only completed for pensioners, not active members
findings.detail: The prior audit recommendation required reconciliation of pension payroll between Altair and Oracle systems. The council completed this for pensioners (the larger cohort) as of 31 March 2025 but did not complete it for active members, so the recommendation has been re-raised. The council commits to completing the full reconciliation for both pensioners and active members in 2025/26.
findings.matters: Incomplete payroll reconciliations are a control weakness in pension fund management that affects the reliability of benefit payments and financial reporting.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: the original recommendation included active members, which the Council did not reconcile, and therefore this has been re-raised. We will then ensure that we undertake this reconciliation for both pensioners and active members as part of the closing for 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Uncorrected audit misstatement of £1.5m in defined benefit obligation due to variance in estimated vs actual benefits paid by pension fund.
findings.detail: Fund actuary used estimated benefits paid (£63,928k) when calculating defined benefit obligation, but actual funded benefits paid were £62,383k, a variance of £1,545k. This remains uncorrected in the financial statements.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether material errors in financial statements indicate control or governance issues. An uncorrected £1.5m misstatement in pension liability, however small in percentage terms, indicates a control gap.
findings.figures: £1,545k variance between estimated and actual pension benefits paid
findings.quote: The fund actuary has used estimated benefits paid while calculating the DBO and DBA liability. An independent confirmation is obtained and noted actual funded benefits are £62,383k as compared to estimated £63,928k. A variance of £1,545k has been noted.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Pension liability £1.4bn with no formalised management review control over actuarial assumptions; auditors performed fully substantive testing rather than relying on controls.
findings.detail: Pension defined benefit obligation of £1,444m (down £218m). Audit identified that there is 'no formalised management review control over the assumptions used in the valuation report' and that the actuarial assumption review process lacks sufficient documentation and criteria for investigation of outliers. Auditors did not rely on management's control and performed fully substantive testing instead.
findings.matters: A lender assesses governance quality over material balance sheet estimates. The absence of effective management review controls over a £1.4bn liability indicates governance weakness and increases reliance on external auditors rather than internal monitoring.
findings.figures: £1,444m gross defined benefit obligation at 31 March 2025; decrease of £218m year-on-year
findings.quote: there is no formalised management review control over the assumptions used in the valuation report

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Council dwellings valuation moved to optimistic position; £1.4bn asset base affected by judgement on small number of beacon properties.
findings.detail: Council dwellings valued at £1,473.6m (£110m increase year-on-year). The audit identified that Housing Price Index indexation used in the valuation (7.6%) was optimistic compared to actual Land Registry data (6.98%). Audit flagged that 'should an error in valuing a small number of beacons arise, it can have a significant impact on the valuation as a whole' for the largest part of the council's land and buildings balance.
findings.matters: A lender assesses asset quality and borrowing capacity against asset base. A £1.4bn valuation that is acknowledged as optimistic, combined with concentration risk in beacon property judgements, affects confidence in balance sheet values.
findings.figures: £1,473.6m valuation of council dwellings at 31 March 2025; HPI indexation used was 7.6%, actual subsequently reduced to 6.98%
findings.quote: our review of the HPI indexation indicated that, as the Land Registry data is subject to a reporting lag due to the timing of completed sales, the percentage movement for the March year-end had subsequently reduced from the 7.6% used in the valuation to 6.98%. This resulted in the estimate appearing optimistic, though it remains within our acceptable range

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Nine of 15 lease agreements could not be located; governance gap in document retention for IFRS 16 transition.
findings.detail: During testing of 15 lease agreements, nine could not be located. This creates risk of disputes and incomplete IFRS 16 disclosures. The council is in the process of consolidating missing lease information, though IFRS 16 audit work remains ongoing at the time of this draft report.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in the completeness and accuracy of financial reporting. Missing lease agreements during IFRS 16 adoption creates risk of material misstatement in balance sheet assets and liabilities.
findings.figures: 9 of 15 sampled lease agreements could not be located
findings.quote: In a sample of 15 lease agreements selected for testing, nine of the agreements could not be located.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Priority 1 control deficiency: system access for leavers not disabled promptly; one leaver account remained active after termination date.
findings.detail: Audit testing identified one instance where a leaver's Oracle account was not disabled on or before the termination date, and file evidence was editable rather than system-generated. Auditors could not obtain direct confirmation from the system that no access occurred after exit. KPMG recommends all leaver accounts be disabled within one business day of termination and system-generated audit evidence be retained.
findings.matters: A lender assesses governance and control environment risk. A Priority 1 control deficiency around access disablement indicates gaps in data security and segregation of duties that could allow fraud or error.
findings.figures: one instance identified in testing sample
findings.quote: we identified one instance where a leaver's user account within the Oracle system was not disabled at or before their termination date

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Council self-referred to Regulator of Social Housing for failure to meet statutory health and safety requirements; 17% of homes still not meeting Decent Homes Standard.
findings.detail: The council brought housing management in-house from its subsidiary in October 2023 and self-referred to the Regulator in December 2023 due to health and safety failures. A stock condition survey found 24% of homes not meeting Decent Homes Standard as at the time of survey; this has improved to 17% (with 87% of stock assessed as of the audit date). The Housing Ombudsman subsequently published a special investigation report identifying five emerging themes of concern.
findings.matters: A lender assesses whether a council can deliver on its service responsibilities and retain grant funding. Self-referral to regulator, housing stock condition failures, and ombudsman investigation signal reputational and financial risk, plus the need for significant capital investment in repairs.
findings.figures: approximately 24% of homes not meeting Decent Homes Standard at initial survey; 17% not meeting standard as at 31 March 2025 (87% of stock assessed)
findings.quote: the Authority subsequently self-referred to the Regulator of Social Housing in December 2023 due to identifying a failure to meet statutory health and safety requirements in some of its properties

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: HRA reserves fell below target and required material rebuild; audit identified specific management override risk on HRA reserves due to deficit pressure.
findings.detail: HRA reserves stood at £7.4m at 31 March 2024, below the target of 10% of rental income. Reserves were topped up to £18.6m in 2024/25 to reach the target level. The audit specifically identified that 'As the Authority is not permitted to be in a HRA fund deficit there is an increased risk of management override which we anticipate could occur by transferring HRA expenditure to the general fund.' This is flagged as a significant fraud risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether a council can respond to service shocks or unexpected costs. HRA reserve pressure and the specific fraud risk flagged by auditors indicates the service is operating with minimal buffer and there is reputational/governance risk.
findings.figures: HRA reserves £7.4m at 31 March 2024 (below 10% target); increased to £18.6m in 2024/25 (now above 10% of rental and service charge income)
findings.quote: As the Authority is not permitted to be in a HRA fund deficit there is an increased risk of management override which we anticipate could occur by transferring HRA expenditure to the general fund.

findings.paper_title: 5. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - London Borough of Lewisham_ISA 260_2024-25_DRAFT 041125
findings.headline: Prior-year accounting error of £40.5m resulted in understated borrowing requirement for HRA capital programme.
findings.detail: The council erroneously recorded £13.9m (2020/21) and £26.6m (2021/22) as revenue contributions to capital outlay when this expenditure should have been financed by borrowing. The prior-year adjustment increased HRA reserves by £39.5m at 1 April 2023 and increased Capital Financing Requirement by £40.5m. This reveals past misrecording of the council's actual borrowing need.
findings.matters: A lender assessing borrowing capacity needs accurate CFR history. This adjustment shows the council's actual borrowing requirement was materially understated for two years, affecting debt forecasting and refinancing decisions.
findings.figures: £40.5m increase to Capital Adjustment Account and Capital Financing Requirement; £39.5m increase to HRA reserves at 1 April 2023; prior years' unrecorded borrowing need of £13.9m (2020/21) and £26.6m (2021/22)
findings.quote: the Authority had erroneously recorded revenue contributions to capital outlay of £13.9m and £26.6m respectively, reducing the HRA CFR in each of those years. This issue was identified in 2025/26 following an investigative review

findings.paper_title: 6. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: £998k valuation overstatement in Level 3 pooled investments due to use of mid prices instead of bid prices
findings.detail: The audit identified an overstatement of £998k in the valuation of LCIV funds, where management used mid prices rather than bid prices for year-end fair value measurement. Under IFRS 13, assets with a bid-ask spread must be valued using the price most representative of fair value. The auditor deemed this not material but classified the Level 3 valuation as 'optimistic' rather than 'balanced'.
findings.matters: Although not material in isolation, this indicates a valuation methodology issue affecting a significant portfolio component (£513.61m in Level 3 investments, 27% of total assets). It suggests potential weakness in fair value assessment processes and control over investment valuations.
findings.figures: £998k overstatement; Level 3 investments £513.61m (27.29% of total £1,882.32m)
findings.quote: This misstatement occurs as management use mid prices report instead of bid prices for year end valuation purpose for LCIV funds. For assets measured at fair value that have a bid and ask price, IFRS 13 requires the use of the price within the bid-ask spread that is the most representative of fair value.

findings.paper_title: 6. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: Priority 1 control deficiency: system access for employee leavers not disabled in timely manner
findings.detail: Audit testing identified one instance where a departing employee's Oracle system account was not disabled promptly after departure. Management could not provide system-generated evidence of disablement; the evidence provided was an editable file that could not be independently verified. The auditor has recommended disabling all leaver accounts within one business day, retaining system-generated audit evidence, and implementing quarterly monitoring.
findings.matters: Failure to revoke system access promptly after employment termination creates fraud and data security risk. Undetected system access by former employees could enable unauthorized transactions, data theft, or financial manipulation. This is a material internal control weakness.
findings.figures: One instance identified
findings.quote: During our testing, we identified one instance where a leaver's user account within the Oracle system was not disabled in a timely manner after the employee's departure... As a result, we were unable to obtain direct system-generated evidence confirming that no access occurred after the employee's exit.

findings.paper_title: 6. Audit and Risk Committee - 11-11-25 - Lewisham Pension Fund_ISA260_2024_25_DRAFT
findings.headline: Priority 1 control deficiency on pension membership reconciliation remains unresolved from prior year audit
findings.detail: The Pension Fund has no formal process to reconcile membership data between the pension system and finance records at year end. This was raised as a priority 1 (fundamental) control deficiency in the prior year with a September 2025 deadline for resolution. As of November 2025 it remains outstanding; the Head of Payroll and Pensions is working with the systems provider to find a solution, indicating the issue has persisted unaddressed for at least four months.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence in internal controls and financial reporting accuracy. Unresolved priority 1 control deficiencies, especially those affecting pension liability data accuracy, indicate a weak control environment and increase fraud and error risk. Pension liabilities are material to the council's balance sheet and may affect the council's finances if deficits need to be funded.
findings.figures: Pension fund total assets £1,882.32m; membership reconciliation issue outstanding since prior year
findings.quote: We noted that no formal member reconciliation is performed noting membership changes in the year, reconciling movements and cross checking against the underlying payroll records. There is a risk that membership information may be incorrect.

findings.paper_title: Minutes Public Pack, 12/06/2025 Pensions Investment Committee
findings.headline: Triennial pension valuation delivered £1.425m saving for 2026/27 through 1% reduction in employers' contribution rate
findings.detail: The Triennial Valuation process for 31 March 2025 has concluded with a positive outcome for the council. The employer contribution rate will reduce by 1%, generating a £1.425m saving for the council's budget in 2026/27. This reduces ongoing pension liabilities and frees cash for other priorities.
findings.matters: Pension contribution savings directly improve the council's cash flow and budgetary headroom; reduced employer contribution rates signal an improved funding position in the pension fund.
findings.figures: £1.425m saving for 2026/27; 1% reduction in Employers' contribution rate
findings.quote: the Council has a saving of £1.425m for 2026/27 predicated on a 1% reduction in the Employers' contribution rate as an outcome from this process

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Triennial valuation results not due until December 2025 or later; funding level and contribution rates remain uncertain
findings.detail: The 2022 valuation set a minimum contribution rate of 17.6%, with the council choosing to pay 22.0%. The next valuation (as at March 2025) will not report results until December 2025 at earliest, or spring 2026. Given the noted impact of inflation and membership maturation on liabilities, and the fund's 3.2% return (0.8% below benchmark), the next valuation may require higher contribution rates.
findings.matters: Lewisham's employer contribution rate may increase significantly from March 2026 onward, creating a budget pressure. The valuation report will also reset the 20-year deficit recovery target and may tighten funding assumptions, forcing earlier deficit closure.
findings.figures: Last valuation (2022): 97% funded, 17.6% minimum contribution rate. Council elected rate: 22.0% for 2024/25. Next valuation results: expected December 2025 or spring 2026.
findings.quote: The next triennial valuation will take place as at March 2025 but the final results are not expected before December 2025.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Hard deadline of 31 March 2026 to transfer all pension fund assets to LCIV pool; currently only 45% pooled
findings.detail: Government reform (announced May 2025) mandates that all LGPS administering authorities transfer asset management to their pool by 31 March 2026. Lewisham currently has only 45% of £1.88bn (£851m) invested in pooled funds, leaving £1.05bn still to be transferred. The report notes 'considerable effort' will be required and changes to PIC's role once pooling is complete.
findings.matters: A hard March 2026 deadline for moving £1bn+ of assets creates execution risk. Failure to meet the deadline invites government direction of the fund to a different pool. Successfully pooling 55% of assets in eight months is operationally complex and could disrupt market positioning.
findings.figures: Total fund: £1.88bn. Pooled assets: £851m (45%). Pooled assets requiring transfer: ~£1.03bn (55%). Deadline: 31 March 2026.
findings.quote: Lewisham continues to work with the LCIV to increase the proportion of its assets that are pooled, (currently 45% pooled) in line with Government expectations for Funds to pool by 31 March 2026

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: No internal audit of pension fund in 2024/25; oversight gap before next triennial valuation
findings.detail: Internal audit did not carry out an inspection in 2024/25. The last audit (2020/21) found 'limited assurance' with recommendations on pension payment accuracy and contribution reconciliation. No inspection occurred this year, leaving a governance gap in the year immediately before the triennial valuation results are finalised (expected December 2025).
findings.matters: The absence of internal audit in 2024/25 creates a control gap in a fund managing £1.88bn. Lenders and audit committees expect continuous oversight; a one-year audit gap before a valuation is a red flag for governance weakness.
findings.figures: Last audit: 2020/21. Next audit: 2025/26. Valuation results expected: December 2025.
findings.quote: Internal Audit did not carry out an inspection in 2024/25 but will be reviewing the practices and procedures in 2025/26.

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Contribution non-payment from admitted bodies: several employers paying 0% or low percentages of required contributions
findings.detail: Several admitted bodies failed to pay their required pension contributions. Aurora Nexus paid 0% of due contributions; RCCN Ltd Hatcham paid 0%; RCCN Ltd Knights paid 0%; CK Bless paid 42%; Super Kids paid 50%. Two employers (RCCN Hatcham and RCCN Knights) had ceased by May 2024, but pension liabilities remain. Phoenix paid only 8%. This represents a significant collection problem.
findings.matters: Non-payment of pension contributions means the Fund either carries the liability unfunded or the council must cover the shortfall. Admitted bodies are often sub-contractors or outsourced services; widespread non-payment suggests financial distress in parts of the council's supply chain.
findings.figures: Aurora Nexus: 0% of £15k due; RCCN Ltd Hatcham: 0% of £17k due; RCCN Ltd Knights: 0% of £5k due; CK Bless: 42% of £3k due; Super Kids: 50% of £1k due; Phoenix: 8% of £305k due.
findings.quote: Phoenix  305 8% ... Aurora Nexus 15 0% ... RCCN Ltd Hatcham 17 0% ... RCCN Ltd Knights 5 0%

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Administration expenses surged 24.8% in a single year, driven by operational cost increases
findings.detail: Pension administration costs rose from £1,111k to £1,387k (£276k increase). Oversight and governance costs rose 28.7% (£128k). The report attributes this to unspecified pressures on local government finances, yet staffing remained at 9.5 FTE, pushing more work onto the same team managing 27,580 members.
findings.matters: Sharp cost rises on a stable staffing base signal pressure in the pension administration function. Lenders monitor council cost control; a 25% cost spike in one year suggests budget discipline issues.
findings.figures: Administration expenses: £1,387k (2024/25) vs £1,111k (2023/24), +£276k (+24.8%). Oversight and governance: £574k vs £446k, +£128k (+28.7%). Staffing: 9.5 FTE for 27,580 members.
findings.quote: Administration Expenses 1,387 1,111 276 24.8%

findings.paper_title: 5a.Appendix 1. Pension Fund Annual Report 2024-25
findings.headline: Active pension contributors declining while Fund liabilities grow due to demographic maturation
findings.detail: Active scheme members fell from 6,888 to 6,728 (160 contributors lost), whilst deferred and retired members increased, pushing the fund toward a declining contribution base. The Executive Director explicitly warns that with 'the prospect of fewer members making contributions in the future, the Fund may have to take more risk to meet its liabilities.'
findings.matters: Declining contributor numbers whilst liabilities grow increase the council's pension funding burden and reduce the funding stability that underpins pension sustainability.
findings.figures: Active members: 6,728 (down from 6,888 in 2023/24). Total membership: 27,580 (down 191). Deferred members: 11,856; Retired: 8,996.
findings.quote: as the Membership of the Fund continues to mature and amidst a prolonged period of higher inflation, both of which increase the Fund's liabilities

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham forecasts £10.0m high needs overspend for 2026/27 as children with EHCPs rise to 4,032
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council is forecasting a £10.0m overspend in 2026/27 on high needs, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. Its period 6 monitoring report to the Public Accounts Select Committee says "there are now 4,032 children with an EHCP", an education, health and care plan. That is 231 more than the 3,801 in September 2025.

The paper gives average placement costs of £15k a year for children placed in the borough and £27k for those placed outside it. The council's cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, stood at £24.4m at 31 March 2026. The statutory override, a government rule that lets councils keep such a deficit off their main balance sheet, "has been extended to 31st March 2028".

Table 11 of the report shows a deficit of £34.0m at the end of 2026/27, and £34.4m for the high needs block. The paper does not reconcile the two figures. The Department for Education (DfE) notified the council on 5 October 2026 that "the DfE has deferred the decision on the SEND Reform Plan". The council must resubmit the plan by the end of November 2026, with a decision expected in January 2027. The paper says the plan could bring grant of up to 90% of eligible expenditure, and that it is unclear what support will be given for the remaining deficit.
news_drafts.paper_title: 6. Period 6 Monitoring Report Draft - PASC Copy

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham forecasts £9.9m gross overspend for 2026/27, £7.0m after mitigations, with £9.7m of savings undelivered
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council is forecasting a gross overspend of £9.9m on its 2026/27 outturn, according to papers for the Children and Young People Select Committee on 11 November. After mitigations, the net overspend for the year is £7.0m.

The figures come from the council's monitoring at period 4, presented to the Mayor and Cabinet in October 2026. The paper says that within the overspend there is "£9.7m of savings not being delivered". The Children and Young People savings report says the council continues to monitor and forecast its outturn. It gives the gross figure without setting out how the overspend will be funded.

The monitoring paper says officers are working to identify which part of the 2026/27 overspend will persist into 2027/28. The papers give no breakdown of the overspend by service and no figure for that part.

news_drafts.headline: Lewisham's 2027/28 budget report to assume up to £30m of reserves for any savings shortfall
news_drafts.lead:
Lewisham Council's 2027/28 budget report will be written on the basis that up to £30m of reserves will be needed to cover any savings shortfall. That is set out in a savings report before the Safer Stronger Communities Select Committee, which meets on 10 November 2026. The report's appendix calls this a fallback position pending agreement of further proposals.

The cover report says the proposals put forward so far do not meet the budget gap. Officers will continue to work up new proposals totalling at least £20m, to be developed as part of setting the 2027/28 budget. The report gives the aim as minimising the risk of needing reserves to set a balanced budget next year.

The appendix also covers what happens to any shortfall. If proposals totalling £30m cannot be identified or agreed, it says, the difference falls to reserves for 2027/28 and "will immediately be added to the 2028/29 savings target which is already £13.985m." It adds that the 2027/28 budget will be set using reserves to the extent of any shortfall as a minimum.
